title: Part 1, Chapter 1
paragraphs: About the character and pursuits of the famous gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha

In a village in La Mancha — the name of which I'd rather not recall — there lived not long ago one of those gentlemen who keep a lance in the rack, an old shield, a lean hack, and a greyhound for hunting. A stew of rather more beef than mutton, a salad most nights, leftovers on Saturdays, lentils on Fridays, and an extra pigeon on Sundays ate up three-quarters of his income. The rest went on a fine wool doublet, velvet breeches with matching shoes for holidays, and his best homespun for weekdays, in which he cut a respectable figure. His household included a housekeeper past forty, a niece under twenty, and a lad who could both saddle the horse and handle the pruning-hook out in the fields and at market. Our gentleman was nearly fifty; he was lean, sinewy, sharp-featured, an early riser and a great hunter. They say his surname was Quixada — or Quesada; the authorities differ — though reasonable inference suggests he was actually called Quexana. This is of little importance to the story; it's enough that the telling not stray a hair's breadth from the truth.

You should know, then, that this gentleman, whenever he had time on his hands (which was most of the year), gave himself over to reading chivalric romances with such enthusiasm and addiction that he almost entirely neglected his hunting and even the management of his property. His mania reached the point where he sold off acres of tilled land to buy more romances, and he brought home every one he could lay hands on. Of all of them, none pleased him more than the work of the famous Feliciano de Silva, whose clarity of style and tangled conceits struck him as pearls beyond price — especially when he came upon the courtship scenes and challenges, where he routinely found passages like "_the reason of the unreason with which my reason is afflicted so weakens my reason that with reason I murmur at your beauty;_" or again, "_the high heavens, that of your divinity divinely fortify you with the stars, render you deserving of the desert your greatness deserves_." Over conceits of that kind the poor gentleman lost his mind, lying awake trying to unpick them and force the meaning out — meaning that Aristotle himself, brought back to life for the purpose, could not have extracted. He was not at all easy about the wounds that Don Belianis gave and took, because however great the surgeons who patched him up, he had to be scarred and seamed from head to toe. But he approved of how the author ended his book with the promise of that interminable adventure, and was many a time tempted to pick up his pen and finish it himself along the lines the text suggests — which he no doubt would have done, and done well, if greater and more absorbing thoughts had not kept getting in the way.

He had many an argument with the village priest (a learned man, a Sigüenza graduate) over which had been the greater knight, Palmerin of England or Amadis of Gaul. Master Nicholas, the village barber, would maintain that neither could touch the Knight of Phoebus, and that if anyone could compare with _him_, it was Don Galaor, Amadis's brother — because Galaor had a spirit equal to any occasion, was no fussy or weepy knight like Amadis, and lost nothing to him in raw valour. In short, our gentleman became so absorbed in his books that he was reading from sunset to sunrise and from dawn till dark, and what with little sleep and constant reading his brain dried out and he lost his wits altogether. His head filled up with what he had been reading — enchantments, quarrels, battles, challenges, wounds, courtships, loves, agonies, and every variety of impossible nonsense — and the whole fabric of invention he had read of took on the weight of truth in his mind, so that to him no history in the world was more real. He used to say that the Cid Ruy Diaz was a very fine knight, but no match for the Knight of the Burning Sword, who with a single backstroke cut two ferocious giants in half. He thought even better of Bernardo del Carpio because at Roncesvalles he killed the enchanted Roland, using Hercules's trick of strangling Antaeus, son of Earth, in his arms. He had great respect for the giant Morgante because, although of the giant breed (which is always arrogant and badly behaved), Morgante alone was affable and well brought up. But above all he admired Reinaldos of Montalbán, especially when Reinaldos rode out from his castle and robbed everyone he met, and when, overseas, he stole that image of Mohammed that the history says was solid gold. For a chance to kick the traitor Ganelon around, he would have handed over his housekeeper, and his niece into the bargain.

In short, his wits being completely gone, he hit upon the strangest notion any madman ever hit upon: that it was both right and necessary — both for his own honour and the service of his country — to turn himself into a knight-errant, ride out into the world in full armour in search of adventures, and put into practice everything he had read of as the standard business of knights-errant — righting every kind of wrong, exposing himself to dangers from which, in the end, he would earn undying fame and renown. The poor man already saw himself crowned at the very least Emperor of Trebizond by the might of his arm; and so, carried away by the sheer pleasure of these fancies, he set about putting his plan into action immediately.

The first thing he did was clean up some armour that had belonged to his great-grandfather and had been lying forgotten in a corner for generations, eaten with rust and covered with mildew. He scoured and polished it as best he could, but he could see one major defect: it had no closed helmet, only a simple morion. He compensated with ingenuity, contriving a kind of half-helmet out of pasteboard that, fitted over the morion, looked like the real thing. True, when he drew his sword to test whether it would stand a cut, the first slash undid in an instant what had taken him a week to make. The ease with which he had reduced it to pieces left him uneasy, so to be safe he rebuilt it, this time fixing iron strips on the inside until he was satisfied with its strength; and then, not caring to run any more experiments, he accepted it as a helmet of the most perfect construction.

He next turned to inspect his horse, which — with more cracks in its hooves than a worn-out coin and more blemishes than Gonela's old nag, _tantum pellis et ossa fuit_ — in his eyes surpassed Alexander's Bucephalus or the Cid's Babieca. Four days were spent thinking up a name, on the grounds (as he said to himself) that it would not be right for a horse belonging to so famous a knight, with such merits of his own, to go without a distinguished name; and he wanted the name to indicate both what the horse had been before he belonged to a knight-errant and what he was now, since it was only fair that, the master taking a new role, the horse take a new name to match — something lofty and full-sounding, suited to the new order and calling he was about to follow. So after composing, crossing out, rejecting, adding to, unmaking, and remaking a great many names out of his memory and imagination, he settled on calling him Rocinante: a name, to his ear, lofty, sonorous, and significant of the horse's condition as a previous hack and his present standing as the first and foremost of all the hacks in the world.

Having found a name for his horse that pleased him, he wanted one for himself, and he spent eight more days on the question, finally settling on "Don Quixote" — from which, as has been mentioned, the authors of this truthful history have inferred that his name must beyond doubt have been Quixada, and not Quesada as some claim. Recalling, though, that the valiant Amadis was not satisfied to be called simply Amadis but added the name of his kingdom and country to make it famous — Amadis of Gaul — he likewise resolved, as a good knight, to attach his own region's name to his own, and to style himself Don Quixote of La Mancha. That, he reckoned, gave an accurate account of his origin and country and did honour to it by taking his surname from it.

So, with his armour polished, his morion converted into a helmet, his horse christened, and himself confirmed, he concluded that nothing further was needed except to find a lady to be in love with; for a knight-errant without love was like a tree without leaves or fruit, or a body without a soul. He said to himself, "If, for my sins — or by my good fortune — I come across some giant out here, which is a normal thing for knights-errant, and unhorse him at the first charge, or split him in two at the waist, or in short defeat and subdue him, won't it be useful to have someone to send him to as a gift, so that he may come in and fall on his knees before my sweet lady and say, in a humble, submissive voice, 'I am the giant Caraculiambro, lord of the island of Malindrania, vanquished in single combat by the never sufficiently praised knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, who has commanded me to present myself before Your Grace, that your Highness may dispose of me at your pleasure'?" Oh, how our gentleman enjoyed this little speech, especially when he had thought of someone to name as his Lady! There was, the story says, in a village near his own, a very good-looking farm girl whom he had once been in love with — though, as far as anyone knows, she never noticed and certainly never gave it a thought. Her name was Aldonza Lorenzo, and he decided to promote her to Lady of his Thoughts. After hunting for a name in keeping with hers, one that would suggest a princess and great lady, he settled on Dulcinea del Toboso (she being from El Toboso): a name, to his mind, musical, uncommon, and significant, like all the others he had already bestowed on himself and on the things belonging to him.

title: Part 1, Chapter 2
paragraphs: About the first sally the ingenious Don Quixote made from home

With these preliminaries settled, he wasn't about to put off his plan any longer, pushed on by the thought of how much the world was losing through his delay — given all the wrongs he meant to right, grievances to redress, injustices to repair, abuses to remove, and duties to discharge. So without telling anyone of his intention and without anyone seeing him, one morning before daybreak (on one of the hottest days of July) he put on his armour, mounted Rocinante with his patched-up helmet on his head, braced his shield, took up his lance, and rode out by the back gate of his yard onto the open plain — overjoyed and entirely satisfied to see how easily he had set his grand purpose in motion. But hardly had he reached the open ground when a terrible thought hit him — one that almost made him abandon the whole enterprise at the start. It occurred to him that he had never been formally dubbed a knight, and that under the law of chivalry he neither could nor should bear arms against any other knight; and that even if he had been dubbed, he ought, as a novice, to wear white armour with no device on his shield until he had earned one by his prowess. These reflections shook him, but his obsession was stronger than any reasoning, and he decided to have himself knighted by the first person he ran into, in line with the example of others in the same fix as he had read of in the books that had brought him to this point. As for the white armour, he resolved to scrub his at the first opportunity until it was whiter than an ermine; and with that reassurance he rode on, letting his horse pick the way, for he believed this was the essence of adventures.

So our newly minted adventurer made his way along, talking to himself: "Who knows but that in the days to come, when the true history of my famous deeds is published, the wise scholar who writes it, when he comes to set down my first sally in the early morning, will do it in this fashion? 'Scarcely had ruddy Apollo spread over the broad face of the earth the golden threads of his bright hair, scarcely had the little birds of painted plumage tuned their voices to greet with sweet and mellifluous harmony the coming of rosy Dawn — who, deserting the soft bed of her jealous husband, was showing herself to mortals at the gates and balconies of the Manchegan horizon — when the renowned knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, leaving the soft down behind, mounted his celebrated steed Rocinante and began to ride across the ancient and famous Campo de Montiel.'" Which in fact he was riding across. "Happy the age, happy the time," he went on, "in which my famous deeds shall be made known, worthy to be cast in bronze, carved in marble, painted in pictures, for a memorial forever. And you, O wise enchanter, whoever you may be, to whom it shall fall to be the chronicler of this strange history, do not, I beg you, forget my good Rocinante, the constant companion of all my travels." Then he broke out again, as if love-struck in earnest: "O Princess Dulcinea, lady of this captive heart, you have done me a terrible wrong to dismiss me with scorn and, by your harsh decree, banish me from the presence of your beauty. O lady, deign to remember this heart that is your vassal — that suffers such sorrow for love of you."

So he kept stringing together absurdities like this in the style his books had taught him, imitating their language as best he could, and meanwhile he rode so slowly and the sun climbed so quickly and beat down so fiercely that it would have been enough to melt his brains if he had any to melt. He travelled nearly all day without anything notable happening, which left him in despair, for he was anxious to encounter someone he could try the strength of his arm on.

There are writers who say his first adventure was the one at Puerto Lapice; others say it was the windmills. But what I have been able to establish, and find written in the annals of La Mancha, is that he was on the road all day, and towards nightfall both he and his horse were dead tired and starving. Looking around for some castle or shepherd's hut where he could refresh himself and ease his needs, he spotted an inn not far off the road — as welcome to him as a star guiding him to the gates, if not the palace, of his salvation; and he picked up the pace and reached it just as night was falling. At the door stood two young women, working girls (as they call them) on their way to Seville with some carriers who had stopped at the inn for the night; and since everything Don Quixote saw or thought of seemed to him to fit the books he'd read, the moment he saw the inn he pictured it as a castle with four turrets, pinnacles of polished silver, and the usual drawbridge, moat, and other castle furniture. Towards this inn, which to him was a castle, he advanced; and stopping Rocinante a short distance off, he waited for some dwarf to appear on the battlements and announce his arrival by sounding a trumpet. But when no one obliged and Rocinante was getting impatient for the stable, he rode up to the inn door and saw the two cheerful young women, who looked to him like two beautiful maidens or noble ladies taking the air at the gate of the castle.

Just then a swineherd, gathering his pigs from the stubble (and that is what they are called, with no apology), blew a blast on his horn to bring them together, and at once it seemed to Don Quixote to be exactly what he was expecting: some dwarf announcing his arrival. So with enormous satisfaction he rode up to the inn and the ladies, who, seeing a man approach in full armour with lance and shield, were starting to retreat into the inn in fright when Don Quixote — guessing their alarm from their flight — raised his pasteboard visor, revealed his dry, dusty face, and addressed them in a courteous tone: "Your ladyships need not run away or fear any rudeness, for the order of knighthood I profess does not permit me to offer any to anyone, least of all to high-born maidens of the kind your appearance proclaims you to be." The girls were staring, trying to make out his features behind the clumsy visor; but when they heard themselves called maidens, which was so far from their actual line of work, they could not keep from laughing. That made Don Quixote indignant, and he said, "Modesty becomes the fair, and what's more, laughter with no real cause behind it is great silliness. But I do not say this to hurt or anger you, for my one desire is to be of service."

The incomprehensible language and unpromising look of our knight only made the girls laugh harder, which made him angrier, and things might have got out of hand if the innkeeper had not come out at that moment. He was a very fat man and therefore a very peaceful one. He, seeing this grotesque figure in armour that matched none of its parts — saddle, bridle, lance, shield, or breastplate — was not at all inclined to join the girls in their laughter; but, in fact, a little nervous of so much hardware, he thought it wise to speak smoothly, so he said, "Señor Caballero, if your worship is looking for a room — bed apart, since there is none in the inn — we have plenty of everything else here." Don Quixote, noting the respectful manner of the Alcaide of the fortress (so the innkeeper and inn seemed to him), replied, "Sir Castellan, anything will do for me, for
'My armour is my only wear, my only rest the fray.'"

The host imagined he was being called Castellan because he took him for a worthy Castilian, though he was in fact an Andalusian from the beach at Sanlúcar — as crafty a thief as Cacus and as full of tricks as a student or a page. "In that case," said he,
"'Your bed is on the flinty rock, your sleep to watch alway;'

and if so, you can dismount and count on plenty of sleeplessness under this roof for a twelvemonth, never mind a single night." Saying this, he stepped over to hold the stirrup for Don Quixote, who dismounted with great difficulty and effort (he hadn't eaten all day), and then asked his host to take good care of his horse, which was the finest piece of horseflesh that ever ate bread in this world. The innkeeper looked Rocinante over and did not find him anywhere near as good as Don Quixote said, nor half as good; and after putting him in the stable, he came back to see what his guest wanted. By now the girls had made their peace with Don Quixote and were helping him off with his armour. They had taken off his breastplate and backpiece, but they didn't know how to undo his gorget or remove his makeshift helmet, which he had tied on with green ribbons whose knots were so tangled they would have to be cut. This Don Quixote refused absolutely to allow, so he kept his helmet on all evening, the strangest and drollest figure imaginable. While they relieved him of the rest of his armour, he took the cheap pair who were doing it for ladies of high rank in the castle, and addressed them, sprightly as ever:
"Oh, never, surely, was there knight so served by hand of dame as served was he, Don Quixote hight, when from his town he came; with maidens waiting on himself, princesses on his hack —

— or Rocinante, for that, ladies, is my horse's name, and Don Quixote of La Mancha my own. I had no intention of declaring myself until my deeds in your service and honour had announced me, but the need to adapt that old ballad of Lancelot to the present occasion has given you my name a little prematurely. There will, however, be a time when your ladyships will command and I will obey, and then the strength of my arm will show how much I wish to serve you."

The girls were not used to this kind of rhetoric and had no reply; they only asked if he wanted something to eat. "I would happily eat something," said Don Quixote, "for I feel it would come at a useful moment." The day happened to be a Friday, and the only food in the entire inn was some pieces of the fish that is called in Castile _abadejo_, in Andalusia _bacallao_, in some places _curadillo_, and in others _troutlet_; so they asked if he could manage troutlet, since they had nothing else to offer. "If there are enough troutlets," said Don Quixote, "they will come to the same thing as a trout, for it's all one to me whether I am given eight reals in small change or a single piece of eight; and besides, these troutlets may be like veal — better than beef — or kid, which is better than goat. Whatever it is, let it come quickly, for the weight and labour of arms cannot be borne without support to the inside." They set up a table for him at the door of the inn, for the air, and the innkeeper brought him a portion of poorly soaked and worse cooked stockfish and a piece of bread as black and mouldy as his armour. It was a laughable sight to see him eat, for with his helmet on and the beaver up, he could not put anything into his mouth with his own hands; someone else had to feed him, and one of the ladies did that. To give him anything to drink would have been impossible, had the landlord not bored out a reed, put one end in his mouth, and poured the wine through the other — all of which Don Quixote endured rather than have the ribbons of his helmet cut.

While this was going on, a hog-gelder came up to the inn and announced his arrival with four or five blasts on his reed pipe — which completely convinced Don Quixote that he was in some famous castle and that they were entertaining him with music, that the stockfish was trout, the bread the whitest wheat, the working girls noble ladies, and the innkeeper the castellan of the castle. He concluded that his enterprise and his first sally had been worth the trouble. But it still distressed him that he had not yet been formally dubbed a knight, since it was clear he could not lawfully take on any adventure without first receiving the order of knighthood.

title: Part 1, Chapter 3
paragraphs: In which the droll way Don Quixote had himself dubbed a knight is described

Worn down by this thought, he hurried through his cheap inn supper, called for the innkeeper, shut himself with him in the stable, and fell on his knees in front of him, saying, "Valiant knight, I will not rise from this spot until your courtesy grants me a favour I am about to ask — a favour that will redound to your praise and the benefit of all humanity." The innkeeper, seeing his guest at his feet and hearing this kind of talk, stood staring, baffled, not sure what to do or say, and kept urging him to get up — but he wouldn't, until the innkeeper agreed to grant the favour. "I expected no less, my lord, of your high magnanimity," replied Don Quixote, "and I have to tell you that the favour I asked, and your generosity has granted, is that tomorrow morning you will dub me a knight, and that tonight I will watch my armour in the chapel of this castle of yours; so that tomorrow, as I have said, what I so much desire will be accomplished, enabling me to roam lawfully throughout all four quarters of the world in search of adventures on behalf of those in distress, as is the duty of chivalry and of knights-errant such as myself, whose ambition is bent on deeds of that kind."

The innkeeper, who, as has been mentioned, was something of a joker, and had already suspected his guest of being out of his wits, was now sure of it on hearing this. To make the evening more amusing, he decided to play along. So he told Don Quixote that he was quite right to pursue this object, and that such a motive was natural and becoming in cavaliers as distinguished as he plainly was; and that he himself, in his younger days, had followed the same honourable calling, ranging in quest of adventures in various parts of the country — the Curing-grounds of Málaga, the Isles of Riarán, the Compass of Seville, the Little Market of Segovia, the Olivera of Valencia, the Rondilla of Granada, the Strand of Sanlúcar, the Colt of Córdoba, the Taverns of Toledo, and various other neighbourhoods, where he had tested the lightness of his feet and the nimbleness of his fingers — doing many wrongs, cheating many widows, ruining a fair number of maidens, swindling minors, and in short bringing himself to the attention of nearly every tribunal and court of justice in Spain — until at last he had retired to this castle of his, where he was living on his own income and other people's, and where he received all knights-errant of whatever rank or condition, out of the great love he bore them, and so that they might share their funds with him in return for his hospitality. He further told him that this castle of his had no chapel where he could keep vigil over his armour, because it had been pulled down for rebuilding; but that in an emergency it could be kept anywhere, and he could keep watch tonight in a courtyard, and in the morning, God willing, the proper ceremonies would be performed and he would be dubbed a knight — and so thoroughly dubbed that no one in the world would be more so. He asked if he had any money on him, to which Don Quixote replied that he did not have a penny, since in the histories of knights-errant he had never read of any of them carrying any. The innkeeper told him he was mistaken: although it was not mentioned in the histories — because in the authors' opinion there was no need to mention something as obvious and necessary as money and clean shirts — it was not therefore to be supposed they did without them, and he could take it as certain and established that all knights-errant (about whom there were so many lengthy and trustworthy books) carried well-stocked purses for emergencies, and also carried shirts and a small box of ointment to treat the wounds they received. For on those plains and in those deserts where they fought and came out wounded, there was not always someone to bandage them up, unless they had as a friend some wise enchanter who would send them help on the spot, fetching through the air on a cloud some damsel or dwarf with a flask of water of such power that a single drop would cure all their hurts on the instant and leave them as sound as if nothing had happened. But in case that didn't happen, the knights of old took care to see their squires were provided with money and other necessities, such as lint and ointments for healing; and when knights had no squires (which was rare), they themselves carried everything in cunning saddle-bags so small they hardly showed on the horse's croup, as if they were something else of more importance — because, except for some such reason, carrying saddle-bags was not very well thought of among knights-errant. He therefore advised him (and, as his godson-to-be, he might even command him) never from that day forward to travel without money and the usual necessities, and he would find the benefit of them when he least expected it.

Don Quixote promised to follow this advice to the letter, and it was arranged at once that he should keep vigil over his armour in a large yard at one side of the inn. So, gathering it all together, Don Quixote laid it on a trough that stood beside a well, braced his shield on his arm, took up his lance, and with a stately air began to march up and down in front of the trough. As he began his patrol, night began to fall.

The innkeeper told everyone at the inn about his guest's craze, the watching of the armour, and the dubbing ceremony he was planning. Astonished at so strange a form of madness, they came out to see from a distance, and watched as he sometimes paced up and down with composure, sometimes leaned on his lance and stared at his armour without taking his eyes off it for the longest time. Night closed in with a moonlight so bright it might have rivalled the sun that loaned it, so that everything the new knight did was clearly seen by everyone.

Meanwhile, one of the carriers at the inn took it into his head to water his team, and to do so it was necessary to move Don Quixote's armour off the trough. Don Quixote, seeing him approach, called out in a loud voice, "O you, whoever you are, rash knight who comes to lay hands on the armour of the most valiant knight-errant that ever girt on a sword — beware what you do; do not touch it, unless you wish to pay for your rashness with your life." The carrier paid no attention to these words (he would have been better off if he had), but grabbed the armour by the straps and flung it some distance away. Seeing this, Don Quixote raised his eyes to heaven, fixed his thoughts (apparently) on his lady Dulcinea, and exclaimed, "Help me, my lady, in this first encounter offered to this breast you hold in thrall; let your favour and protection not fail me in this first peril." With these and other words to the same effect, he dropped his shield, lifted his lance with both hands, and brought it down on the carrier's head with such force that he laid him out on the ground; one more such blow would have spared the surgeon a job. Done with that, he picked up his armour and returned to his patrol with the same serenity as before.

Shortly after, another carrier, not knowing what had happened (the first still lay senseless), came with the same intention of watering his mules, and was about to move the armour off the trough when Don Quixote — without a word or a call for help — once again dropped his shield, lifted his lance, and without quite cracking the second carrier's head open made three or four pieces of it, splitting it in four places. At the noise the whole inn came running, the innkeeper with them. Seeing this, Don Quixote braced his shield on his arm, put his hand on his sword, and exclaimed, "O Lady of Beauty, strength and support of my fainting heart, it is time to turn the eyes of your greatness upon this your captive knight on the brink of so mighty an adventure." That inspired him enough that he would not have flinched if all the carriers in the world had attacked him. The companions of the wounded, seeing the state they were in, began at a distance to rain stones down on Don Quixote, who shielded himself as best he could, not daring to leave the trough and abandon his armour. The innkeeper shouted at them to leave him alone, saying he had already told them the man was mad, and as a madman he would not be held to account even if he killed every one of them. Don Quixote shouted louder, calling them knaves and traitors, and calling the lord of the castle — for letting knights-errant be treated in this way — a villain and a base-born knight, whom, had he himself been knighted, he would call to account for his treachery. "But of you," he cried, "base and vile rabble, I take no notice. Throw, strike, come on — do whatever you can against me; you'll see the reward of your folly and insolence." He said this with such force and boldness that he filled his attackers with real fear, and as much for that reason as because of the innkeeper's pleas, they stopped stoning him. He allowed them to carry off the wounded, and with the same calm and composure as before resumed the watch over his armour.

But these antics of his guest did not at all please the innkeeper, who decided to cut the business short and bestow on him at once the wretched order of knighthood before any further mishap could occur. So, going up to him, he apologised for the rudeness which, without his knowledge, had been shown to him by those low people — who, he said, had been well punished for their audacity. As he had already told him, there was no chapel in the castle, but it wasn't needed for what remained to be done; as he understood the ceremony, the whole point of being dubbed a knight lay in the accolade and in the slap on the shoulder, and that could be administered in the middle of a field. He had already done all that was needed by way of watching the armour, since the requirement was satisfied by a two-hour watch, and he had been at it more than four. Don Quixote believed everything and said he stood there ready to obey, asking only that the business be ended as quickly as possible — for, if he were attacked again and felt himself dubbed a knight, he didn't think he would leave a soul alive in the castle, except for those he might spare out of respect at the innkeeper's request.

So warned, and so threatened, the castellan brought out a book in which he used to enter the straw and barley he issued to the carriers, and with a boy carrying a candle stub and the two damsels already mentioned, he came back to where Don Quixote stood and ordered him to kneel. Then, reading from his account-book as if he were reciting a prayer, halfway through he raised his hand and gave him a hearty blow on the neck, and after that, with the man's own sword, a smart slap on the shoulder — muttering between his teeth the whole time as though he were at prayer. When this was done, he directed one of the ladies to gird on his sword, which she did with great self-possession and gravity, though it took some doing to keep herself from bursting out laughing at each stage of the ceremony; what they had already seen of the novice knight's prowess kept the laughter in check. As she girded on the sword the good woman said, "May God make your worship a fortunate knight and give you success in battle." Don Quixote asked her name, so that he might know from then on to whom he was indebted for the favour received, since he meant to give her some share of whatever honour he won by the might of his arm. She answered, very humbly, that her name was La Tolosa, and that she was the daughter of a cobbler in Toledo who lived in the stalls of Sanchobienaya, and that wherever she was she would serve and respect him as her lord. Don Quixote replied that she would do him a favour if from now on she took the "Doña" and called herself Doña Tolosa. She promised she would. Then the other buckled on his spur, and with her he had practically the same conversation as with the lady of the sword. He asked her name, and she said it was La Molinera, that she was the daughter of a respectable miller of Antequera; and of her likewise Don Quixote asked that she take the "Doña" and call herself Doña Molinera, with offers of further service and favours.

Having brought these never-before-seen ceremonies to a hasty close, Don Quixote was on tenterhooks until he saw himself in the saddle and on his way out in search of adventures. He saddled Rocinante at once, mounted, and embracing his host, he thanked him for knighting him in language so extravagant that it is impossible to convey it, let alone report it. The innkeeper, to get him out of the inn, replied with no less rhetoric, if in fewer words, and without making him pay the bill let him ride off with a God-speed.

title: Part 1, Chapter 4
paragraphs: About what happened to our knight when he left the inn

Day was breaking when Don Quixote left the inn, so happy, so cheerful, so exhilarated at finding himself a knight at last that his joy was about to burst his horse-girths. But recalling his host's advice about the necessities he ought to carry — especially money and shirts — he decided to ride home, supply himself with all of that, and pick up a squire as well; he had in mind a farm-labourer, a neighbour of his, a poor man with a family, but well qualified to act as squire to a knight. With this in mind he turned his horse's head towards his village, and Rocinante, reminded of his old quarters, stepped out so briskly he seemed scarcely to touch the ground.

He had not gone far when out of a thicket on his right there came what sounded like the faint cries of someone in distress, and the moment he heard them he exclaimed, "Thanks be to heaven for the favour it grants me, in offering me so soon an opportunity to fulfil the obligation I have taken on and reap the fruits of my ambition. These cries, no doubt, come from some man or woman in need of help — needing my aid and protection;" and wheeling, he turned Rocinante in the direction the cries seemed to come from. He had gone only a few paces into the wood when he saw a mare tied to an oak, and tied to another tree, stripped to the waist, a youth of about fifteen, from whom the cries were coming. Nor were they without cause, for a hefty farmer was flogging him with a belt and following up every blow with scoldings and orders, repeating, "Keep your mouth shut and your eyes open!" while the boy kept answering, "I won't do it again, master; by God's passion I won't do it again, and I'll watch the flock more carefully next time."

Seeing what was going on, Don Quixote said in an angry voice, "Discourteous knight, it ill becomes you to attack one who cannot defend himself; mount your steed and take your lance" (for there was a lance leaning against the oak the mare was tied to), "and I will make you understand that what you are doing is the behaviour of a coward." The farmer, seeing this figure in full armour brandishing a lance over his head, gave himself up for dead, and answered meekly, "Sir Knight, this boy I am chastising is my servant, hired by me to watch a flock of sheep nearby; he is so careless that I lose one every day, and when I punish him for his carelessness and dishonesty he says I do it out of stinginess, to dodge paying him the wages I owe him — and before God, on my soul, he lies."

"Lies to my face, you base clown!" said Don Quixote. "By the sun that shines on us I have a mind to run you through with this lance. Pay him at once and not another word; or, by the God that rules us, I will make an end of you and wipe you out on the spot. Release him this instant."
The farmer hung his head, and without a word untied his servant, of whom Don Quixote asked how much his master owed him.
He answered, nine months at seven reals a month. Don Quixote did the arithmetic, found it came to sixty-three reals, and told the farmer to pay it down at once if he didn't want to die for it.

The trembling clown answered that, as he lived and by the oath he had sworn (though he had sworn no such oath), it was not that much; account had to be taken — and deducted — for three pairs of shoes he had given him, and a real for two bloodlettings when he was sick.

"That's all very well," said Don Quixote, "but let the shoes and the bloodlettings stand as a setoff against the beatings you have given him without any cause; for if he wore out the leather of the shoes you paid for, you have damaged the leather of his body, and if the barber drew blood from him when he was sick, you have drawn it when he was healthy. On that score he owes you nothing."
"The difficulty is, Sir Knight, that I have no money on me here; let Andres come home with me and I will pay him every last real."
"Go with him!" cried the boy. "God forbid! No, señor, not for the world; for once alone with me, he'd flay me like Saint Bartholomew."

"He will do nothing of the kind," said Don Quixote; "I have only to command, and he will obey me; and since he has sworn to me by the order of knighthood he has received, I leave him free, and I guarantee the payment."
"Think about what you're saying, señor," said the boy; "this master of mine is not a knight, nor has he received any order of knighthood; he is Juan Haldudo the Rich, of Quintanar."
"That matters little," replied Don Quixote; "there may well be Haldudo knights; besides, every man is the son of his own deeds."
"That's true," said Andres; "but this master of mine — of what deeds is he the son, when he refuses me the wages of my sweat and labour?"

"I don't refuse, brother Andres," said the farmer, "just be good enough to come along with me, and I swear by all the orders of knighthood there are in the world to pay you what was agreed, real by real, and perfumed."

"I'll excuse you the perfume," said Don Quixote; "give it to him in reals and I'll be satisfied; and see that you do as you have sworn. If not, by the same oath I swear to come back and hunt you down and punish you; and I will find you, though you hide closer than a lizard. And if you want to know who lays this command on you, so that you are the more firmly bound to obey, know that I am the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, the undoer of wrongs and injustices; and so, God be with you, and don't forget what you have promised and sworn, under the penalties already declared to you."

Saying this, he spurred Rocinante and was soon out of reach. The farmer followed him with his eyes, and once he saw that he had cleared the wood and was out of sight, he turned to his boy Andres and said, "Come here, son, I want to pay you what I owe you, just as that undoer of wrongs commanded me."

"My oath on it," said Andres, "your worship will be wise to obey the command of that good knight — may he live a thousand years — for as he is a valiant and just judge, by Roque, if you do not pay me he will come back and do as he said."

"My oath on it too," said the farmer; "but as I have such a strong affection for you, I want to add to the debt so I can add to the payment;" and seizing him by the arm, he tied him up again and gave him such a flogging that he left him for dead.

"Now, Master Andres," said the farmer, "call on the undoer of wrongs; you'll find he won't undo that — though I'm not sure I'm quite done with you, since I have a good mind to flay you alive." But in the end he untied him and let him go look for his judge, so the sentence could be put into execution.

Andres set off rather down in the mouth, swearing he would go and find the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha and tell him exactly what had happened, and that all of it would have to be repaid sevenfold; but for all that, he went off weeping, while his master stood laughing.

Thus did the valiant Don Quixote right that wrong, and, thoroughly pleased with how the whole thing had turned out, considering that he had made a very happy and noble beginning to his knighthood, he took the road towards his village in perfect self-content, saying under his breath, "Well may you today call yourself fortunate above all on earth, O Dulcinea del Toboso, fairest of the fair! since it has fallen to your lot to hold subject and submissive to your full will and pleasure a knight so renowned as is, and will be, Don Quixote of La Mancha — who, as all the world knows, only yesterday received the order of knighthood and today has righted the greatest wrong and grievance that ever injustice conceived and cruelty perpetrated; who has today snatched the rod from the hand of that ruthless oppressor so wantonly lashing that tender child."

He now came to a road branching in four directions, and at once he was reminded of those crossroads where knights-errant used to halt to consider which road to take. In imitation of them he stopped for a while, and after deep deliberation he gave Rocinante his head, deferring his own will to that of his hack, who followed out his first intention — making straight for his own stable. After he had gone about two miles, Don Quixote noticed a large party of people, who, as it turned out, were some Toledo traders on their way to buy silk at Murcia. There were six of them coming along under their sunshades, with four mounted servants and three muleteers on foot. The moment Don Quixote spotted them, the fancy seized him that here must be some new adventure; and to help him imitate as nearly as he could the episodes he had read about in his books, this seemed sent expressly for the purpose, and he resolved to take it on. So with a lofty bearing and resolve he planted his feet firmly in the stirrups, got his lance ready, brought his buckler up to his chest, and, planting himself in the middle of the road, stood waiting for these knights-errant to approach — for that is what he now considered and held them to be. When they had come near enough to see and hear, he cried out with a haughty gesture, "All the world stand, unless all the world will confess that in all the world there is no maiden fairer than the Empress of La Mancha, the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso."

The traders halted at this language and the sight of the strange figure delivering it, and from both figure and language they at once guessed the craziness of the speaker; but they wanted to find out quietly what was the point of this confession demanded of them, and one of them, who was fond of a joke and quite quick-witted, said, "Sir Knight, we do not know who this good lady is that you speak of; show her to us, for if she is of such beauty as you suggest, with all our hearts and without any pressure we will confess the truth that you require of us."

"If I were to show her to you," replied Don Quixote, "what credit would there be in your confessing a truth so self-evident? The essential point is that, without seeing her, you must believe, confess, affirm, swear, and defend it; if not, you have me to deal with in battle, ill-conditioned, arrogant rabble that you are. Come at me, one by one as the order of knighthood requires, or all together, as is the custom and vile habit of your kind — here I stand and wait for you, relying on the justice of the cause I uphold."

"Sir Knight," replied the trader, "I beg your worship, in the name of this present company of princes, that to spare us from burdening our consciences with the confession of a thing we have never seen or heard of — and one moreover so much to the prejudice of the Empresses and Queens of the Alcarria and Estremadura — your worship will be pleased to show us some portrait of this lady, even if it be no bigger than a grain of wheat; for by the thread one finds the ball, and that way we'll be satisfied and easy, and you'll be content and pleased. In fact I think we are already so far in agreement with you that even if her portrait showed her blind in one eye, and oozing vermilion and sulphur out of the other, we would, to oblige your worship, still say everything in her favour you could desire."

"She oozes nothing of the kind, you vile rabble," said Don Quixote, burning with rage. "Nothing of the kind, I say — only ambergris and civet in cotton wool; nor is she one-eyed or humpbacked, but straighter than a Guadarrama spindle. But you shall pay for the blasphemy you have uttered against beauty like that of my lady."

And with that, he charged with levelled lance at the man who had spoken, with such fury and ferocity that if luck had not arranged for Rocinante to stumble and fall midway, it would have gone badly for the reckless trader. Down went Rocinante, and over went his master, rolling along the ground for some distance; and when he tried to get up he couldn't, so encumbered was he with lance, buckler, spurs, helmet, and the weight of his old armour. All the while he was struggling to rise, he kept shouting, "Don't run, you cowards and wretches! Stand and fight, for it's not my fault but my horse's that I'm stretched here."

One of the muleteers in the party, who could not have had much good nature in him, hearing the poor man on the ground blustering like this, could not resist giving him an answer on his ribs; and coming up to him, he seized the lance, broke it into pieces, and with one of them began thrashing our Don Quixote so thoroughly that, in spite of his armour, he ground him like a measure of wheat. His masters called out not to lay on so hard and to leave the man alone, but the muleteer's blood was up, and he wasn't dropping the game until he had vented the rest of his rage, and gathering up the remaining fragments of the lance, he finished by hammering them down on the unhappy victim, who all through the storm of sticks that rained on him never stopped threatening heaven, and earth, and the brigands, as they seemed to him. At last the muleteer was tired, and the traders went on their way, taking with them plenty to talk about, in the matter of the poor fellow who had been cudgelled. As for him, finding himself alone, he made another effort to rise; but if he hadn't been able when whole and sound, how was he to rise after being thrashed and well-nigh knocked to pieces? And yet he counted himself lucky, since to his mind this was a regular knight-errant's mishap, and entirely, in his view, the fault of his horse. However, battered in body as he was, getting up was beyond his power.

title: Part 1, Chapter 5
paragraphs: In which the story of our knight's mishap is continued

Finding, then, that he really could not move, he hit upon his usual remedy, which was to think of some passage from his books, and his craze brought to mind the story of Baldwin and the Marquis of Mantua, when Carloto left him wounded on the mountainside — a tale known by heart by every child, not forgotten by the young men, and praised and even believed by the old folk, and for all that no whit truer than the miracles of Mahomet. This seemed to him a perfect fit for the case he was in, so, making a show of severe suffering, he began to roll on the ground and to gasp out the very words the wounded knight of the wood is said to have spoken:
Where art thou, lady mine, that thou My sorrow dost not rue? Thou canst not know it, lady mine, Or else thou art untrue.
And so he went on with the ballad as far as the lines:
O noble Marquis of Mantua, My Uncle and liege lord!

As luck would have it, when he had got this far, there happened along a peasant from his own village, a neighbour of his, who had been to the mill with a load of wheat; and seeing the man stretched there, he came up and asked him who he was and what was the matter that he was groaning so pitifully.

Don Quixote was firmly convinced that this was the Marquis of Mantua, his uncle, so the only reply he made was to keep going with his ballad, telling the tale of his misfortune and of the loves of the Emperor's son and his wife, exactly as the ballad sings it.

The peasant stood astonished at hearing such nonsense, and relieving him of the visor (already battered to pieces by blows), he wiped his face, which was covered with dust; and as soon as he had done so he recognised him and said, "Señor Quixada" (which seems to have been what he was called when he was in his senses and hadn't yet changed from a quiet country gentleman into a knight-errant), "who has brought your worship to this state?" But to every question the other only kept going with his ballad.

Seeing this, the good man removed as best he could his breastplate and backpiece, to see if he had any wound, but could see no blood nor any mark of any kind. He then managed to lift him off the ground, and with no little effort hoisted him onto his ass, which seemed to him the easier mount; and gathering up the arms — even the splinters of the lance — he tied them on Rocinante, and leading Rocinante by the bridle and the ass by the halter, he took the road for the village, very sad at having to listen to the absurd stuff Don Quixote was talking.

Nor was Don Quixote less sad, for what with blows and bruises he could not sit upright on the ass, and from time to time he sent up sighs to heaven loud enough that the peasant had to ask once more what ailed him. And it can only have been the devil himself who put into his head tales to match his own adventures, for now, forgetting Baldwin, he thought of the Moor Abindarraez, when the Alcaide of Antequera, Rodrigo de Narvaez, took him prisoner and carried him off to his castle; so when the peasant asked him again how he was and what ailed him, he replied with the very words and phrases that the captive Abindarraez had used to Rodrigo de Narvaez, exactly as he had read the story in Jorge de Montemayor's "Diana" — applying it to his own situation so neatly that the peasant went along cursing his fate for having to listen to such a load of nonsense. From it, however, he concluded that his neighbour was mad, and pressed on as fast as he could to the village to escape the wearisomeness of Don Quixote's harangue, who, at the end of it, said, "Señor Don Rodrigo de Narvaez, you should know that the fair Xarifa I have mentioned is now the lovely Dulcinea del Toboso, for whom I have done, am doing, and will do the most famous deeds of chivalry that this world has seen, is to see, or ever shall see."

To this the peasant answered, "Señor — sinner that I am! — can your worship not see that I'm not Don Rodrigo de Narvaez nor the Marquis of Mantua, but Pedro Alonso your neighbour, and that your worship is neither Baldwin nor Abindarraez, but the worthy gentleman Señor Quixada?"

"I know who I am," replied Don Quixote, "and I know that I may be not only those I have named, but all the Twelve Peers of France, and even all the Nine Worthies, since my achievements outdo everything they have done — all of them together, and each of them on his own."

With this kind of talk and more like it, they reached the village just as night was beginning to fall, but the peasant waited until it was a little later, so the battered gentleman wouldn't be seen riding in such a miserable state. When the time seemed right to him he entered the village and made for Don Quixote's house, which he found all in confusion. The curate and the village barber, who were great friends of Don Quixote, were there, and his housekeeper was saying to them loudly, "What does your worship think can have happened to my master, Señor Licentiate Pero Perez?" — for so the curate was called. "It is three days now since we've seen anything of him, or the hack, or the buckler, lance, or armour. Wretch that I am! I am certain of it — as sure as I was born to die — that these accursed books of chivalry he has, and has got into the habit of reading constantly, have unhinged his reason; for now I remember many times hearing him say to himself that he meant to turn knight-errant and go all over the world in search of adventures. To the devil and Barabbas with such books, that have ruined in this way the finest mind there was in all La Mancha!"

The niece said the same, and more: "You should know, Master Nicholas" — for that was the barber's name — "it was often my uncle's way to spend two days and nights together poring over those unholy books of misadventures, after which he would fling the book away, snatch up his sword, and fall to slashing the walls; and when he was worn out he would say he had killed four giants like four towers; and the sweat that ran off him when he was exhausted he said was the blood of the wounds he had received in battle. Then he would drink a great jug of cold water and become calm and quiet, saying this water was a most precious potion brought to him by the sage Esquife, a great magician and friend of his. But I take all the blame on myself for never telling your worships of my uncle's vagaries, that you might have put a stop to them before things came to this pass, and burnt all these accursed books — and there are many of them — that richly deserve to be burnt like heretics."

"I say the same," said the curate, "and by my faith tomorrow shall not pass without public judgment on them, and may they be condemned to the flames so they do not lead any other reader to behave as my good friend seems to have behaved."

All this the peasant overheard, and from it he finally grasped what was wrong with his neighbour, so he began calling aloud, "Open, your worships, to Señor Baldwin and to Señor the Marquis of Mantua, who comes badly wounded; and to Señor Abindarraez, the Moor, whom the valiant Rodrigo de Narvaez, the Alcaide of Antequera, brings captive."
At these words they all hurried out, and when they recognised their friend, master, and uncle, who had not yet dismounted from the ass because he couldn't, they ran to embrace him.
"Stop!" he said; "for I am badly wounded through my horse's fault. Carry me to bed, and if possible send for the wise Urganda to look at my wounds and cure them."

"There you go! plague on it!" cried the housekeeper at this. "Didn't my heart tell the truth as to which foot my master was lame of? Off to bed with your worship at once, and we'll contrive to cure you here without fetching any Hurgada. A curse, I say, once more, and a hundred times more, on those books of chivalry that have brought your worship to such a pass."

They carried him to bed at once, and after searching for his wounds could find none, but he said they were all bruises from a heavy fall with his horse Rocinante while in combat with ten giants, the biggest and boldest on earth.
"So, so!" said the curate. "Are there giants in the dance? By the sign of the Cross I will burn them tomorrow before the day is over."

They put a host of questions to Don Quixote, but his only answer to any of them was to give him something to eat and let him sleep, for that was what he needed most. They did so, and the curate questioned the peasant at length about how he had found Don Quixote. He told him, and the nonsense Don Quixote had spouted both when found and on the road home, all of which only made the licentiate the more eager to do what he did the next day — which was to summon his friend the barber, Master Nicholas, and go with him to Don Quixote's house.

title: Part 1, Chapter 6
paragraphs: About the diverting and important inquiry which the curate and the barber made into the library of our ingenious gentleman

He was still asleep, so the curate asked the niece for the keys of the room where the books — the source of all the mischief — were kept, and she gave them up very willingly. They all went in, the housekeeper with them, and found more than a hundred large volumes very well bound, and a number of smaller ones. The moment the housekeeper saw them she turned about and ran out of the room, then came back at once with a saucer of holy water and a sprinkler, saying, "Here, your worship, señor licentiate, sprinkle this room; don't leave any magician of the many there are in these books here to bewitch us in revenge for our plan to banish them from the world."

The housekeeper's simplicity made the licentiate laugh, and he directed the barber to hand him the books one by one, to see what they were about, since some might turn out not to deserve the penalty of fire.

"No," said the niece, "there is no reason to show mercy to any of them; they have all done damage; better fling them out of the window into the courtyard and pile them up and set fire to them; or take them out to the back yard, where the bonfire can be made without the smoke bothering anyone." The housekeeper said the same — they were both that eager for the slaughter of those innocents — but the curate would not agree without first reading at least the titles.

The first that Master Nicholas put into his hands was "The four books of Amadis of Gaul." "This seems a portentous thing," said the curate, "for, as I have heard, this was the first book of chivalry printed in Spain, and from it all the others derive their origin and birth; so it seems to me we should condemn it without appeal to the flames, as the founder of so vile a sect."
"No, sir," said the barber, "I too have heard that this is the best of all the books of this kind that have ever been written, and so, being uniquely fine of its kind, it should be pardoned."
"True," said the curate; "and for that reason let its life be spared for the present. Let's see this other one next to it."
"That," said the barber, "is the 'Sergas de Esplandian,' the lawful son of Amadis of Gaul."

"Then, truly," said the curate, "the father's merit should not be credited to the son. Take it, mistress housekeeper; open the window and fling it into the yard, and lay the foundation of the pile for the bonfire we're going to make."
The housekeeper obeyed with great satisfaction, and the worthy "Esplandian" went flying out into the yard to await with all patience the fire that was in store for him.
"Carry on," said the curate.
"This next one," said the barber, "is 'Amadis of Greece' — and indeed I think all of those on this side are of the same Amadis lineage."

"Then out into the yard with the whole lot of them," said the curate. "To have the burning of Queen Pintiquiniestra, and the shepherd Darinel with his eclogues, and the author's bedevilled and twisted discourses, I would burn the father who begot me along with them if he were going about in the guise of a knight-errant."
"I'm of the same mind," said the barber.
"And so am I," added the niece.
"In that case," said the housekeeper, "here — out into the yard with them!"
They were handed to her, and as there were a lot of them, she spared herself the staircase and flung them down out of the window.
"Who is that fat tub there?" said the curate.
"That," said the barber, "is 'Don Olivante de Laura.'"

"The author of that book," said the curate, "was the same who wrote 'The Garden of Flowers,' and truly there is no deciding which of the two books is the more truthful — or, to put it better, the less lying; all I can say is, send this one into the yard for a swaggering fool."
"This next is 'Florismarte of Hircania,'" said the barber.

"Señor Florismarte here?" said the curate. "Then by my faith he must take up his quarters in the yard, in spite of his marvellous birth and visionary adventures, for the stiffness and dryness of his style deserve nothing else. Out into the yard with him and the other, mistress housekeeper."
"With all my heart, señor," said she, and carried out the order with great delight.
"This," said the barber, "is 'The Knight Platir.'"
"An old book that," said the curate, "but I find no reason for mercy in it; send it after the others without appeal" — which was done.
Another book was opened, and they saw it was titled "The Knight of the Cross."
"For the sake of the holy name this book bears," said the curate, "its ignorance might be excused; but then, they say, 'behind the cross there's the devil' — to the fire with it."
Taking down another book, the barber said, "This is 'The Mirror of Chivalry.'"

"I know his worship," said the curate; "that's where Señor Reinaldos of Montalvan figures with his friends and comrades, greater thieves than Cacus, and the Twelve Peers of France with the veracious historian Turpin. As for them, I'm not for condemning them to more than perpetual banishment, because, at any rate, they have some share in the invention of the famous Matteo Boiardo, from which too the Christian poet Ludovico Ariosto wove his web — and as for him, if I find him here speaking any language but his own, I'll show him no respect whatever; but if he speaks his own tongue, I'll set him on my head."
"Well, I have him in Italian," said the barber, "but I don't understand him."

"Nor would it be a good thing if you did," said the curate; "and on that score we might have excused the Captain too, if he hadn't brought him into Spain and turned him into Castilian. He robbed him of a great deal of his natural force, as do all those who try to render books written in verse into another language: with all their care and cleverness, they can never come up to the originals as first produced. In short, I say that this book — and every other that turns up dealing with those French affairs — should be thrown into, or stored in, some dry well, until after more thought it is settled what to do with them. Always excepting one 'Bernardo del Carpio' that is going about, and another called 'Roncesvalles'; for these, if they come into my hands, shall pass straight into the housekeeper's, and from hers into the fire without reprieve."

To all this the barber gave his assent, and looked on it as right and proper, being convinced that the curate was so staunch a Catholic and loyal to the Truth that he would not for the world say anything against them. Opening another book, he saw it was "Palmerin de Oliva," and beside it was another called "Palmerin of England," at which the licentiate said, "Let the Olive be made firewood of at once and burnt until not even ashes are left; and let that Palm of England be kept and preserved as a thing unique. Let such another case be made for it as the one Alexander found among the spoils of Darius and set aside for the safekeeping of the works of the poet Homer. This book, my friend, is of authority for two reasons: first because it is very good, and second because it is said to have been written by a wise and witty king of Portugal. All the adventures at the Castle of Miraguarda are excellent and ingeniously contrived; the language is polished and clear, and the style suits the speaker with judgment and propriety. So then, if it seems good to you, Master Nicholas, I say let this and 'Amadis of Gaul' be exempted from the penalty of fire, and as for all the rest, let them perish without further question."
"No, my friend," said the barber, "for this that I have here is the famous 'Don Belianis.'"

"Well," said the curate, "that, and the second, third, and fourth parts, all stand in need of a little rhubarb to purge their excess of bile, and they must be cleared of all that business about the Castle of Fame and other greater affectations; to that end let them be allowed the overseas term, and as they mend, so shall mercy or justice be meted out to them. In the meantime, my friend, keep them at your house and let no one read them."

"With all my heart," said the barber; and not caring to tire himself with reading any more books of chivalry, he told the housekeeper to take all the big ones and throw them into the yard. It wasn't said to one dull or deaf, but to one who enjoyed burning them more than weaving the broadest and finest cloth she could make; and seizing about eight at a time, she flung them out of the window.
Carrying so many at once, she let one fall at the barber's feet, who picked it up, curious to know whose it was, and found it said, "History of the Famous Knight, Tirante el Blanco."

"God bless me!" said the curate with a shout. "'Tirante el Blanco' here! Hand it over, friend, for in it I think I have found a treasury of enjoyment and a mine of recreation. Here are Don Kyrieleison of Montalvan, a valiant knight, and his brother Thomas of Montalvan, and the knight Fonseca, with the battle the bold Tirante fought with the mastiff, and the witticisms of the damsel Placerdemivida, and the loves and wiles of the widow Reposada, and the empress in love with the squire Hipolito — in truth, my friend, by right of its style it is the best book in the world. Here knights eat and sleep, and die in their beds, and make their wills before dying, and a great deal more that you'll find nothing of in any of the other books. Nevertheless, I say that whoever wrote it, for deliberately composing such fooleries, deserves to be sent to the galleys for life. Take it home with you and read it, and you'll see what I'm saying is true."
"As you wish," said the barber; "but what shall we do with these little books that are left?"

"These must be, not chivalry, but poetry," said the curate; and opening one he saw it was Jorge de Montemayor's "Diana," and supposing all the others to be of the same sort, he said, "these don't deserve to be burnt like the others, for they neither do nor can do the harm the books of chivalry have done — they are books of entertainment that can hurt no one."

"Ah, señor!" said the niece, "your worship had better order these to be burnt as well as the others; for it would be no wonder if, after being cured of his chivalry disorder, my uncle, by reading these, took it into his head to turn shepherd and roam the woods and fields singing and piping — or, worse still, to turn poet, which they say is an incurable and infectious disease."

"The damsel is right," said the curate, "and it'll be just as well to remove this stumbling block and temptation from our friend's path. To begin, then, with Montemayor's 'Diana.' My opinion is that it shouldn't be burnt, but that it should be cleared of all that business about the sage Felicia and the magic water, and of almost all the longer pieces of verse; let it keep, and welcome, its prose and the honour of being the first of books of its kind."
"This next," said the barber, "is the 'Diana,' titled the 'Second Part, by the Salamancan,' and this other has the same title, and its author is Gil Polo."

"As for that of the Salamancan," replied the curate, "let it go to swell the number of the condemned in the yard, and let Gil Polo's be preserved as if it came from Apollo himself. But get on, my friend, and make haste, for it's getting late."
"This book," said the barber, opening another, "is the ten books of the 'Fortune of Love,' written by Antonio de Lofraso, a Sardinian poet."

"By the orders I have received," said the curate, "since Apollo has been Apollo, and the Muses have been Muses, and poets have been poets, no book so funny and absurd as this has ever been written; in its way it is the best and most singular of any of its species that has appeared so far, and whoever has not read it may be sure he has never read what is truly delightful. Give it here, friend, for I make more of having found it than if they had given me a cassock of Florentine stuff."
He set it aside with the greatest satisfaction, and the barber went on, "These next are 'The Shepherd of Iberia,' 'Nymphs of Henares,' and 'The Enlightenment of Jealousy.'"
"Then all we have to do," said the curate, "is hand them over to the secular arm of the housekeeper — and ask me not why, or we shall never have done."
"This next is the 'Pastor de Fílida.'"
"No Pastor that," said the curate, "but a highly polished courtier; let it be preserved as a precious jewel."
"This large one here," said the barber, "is called 'The Treasury of various Poems.'"

"If there weren't so many of them," said the curate, "they would be more relished. This book must be weeded and cleansed of certain vulgarities it has alongside its excellences; let it be preserved because the author is a friend of mine, and out of respect for the other, more heroic and loftier works he has written."
"This," continued the barber, "is the 'Cancionero' of Lopez de Maldonado."

"The author of that book, too," said the curate, "is a great friend of mine, and his verses from his own mouth are the admiration of all who hear them, for such is the sweetness of his voice that he enchants when he chants them. It gives rather too much space to its eclogues, but what is good has never yet been plentiful: let it be kept with those that have been set aside. But what book is that next to it?"
"The 'Galatea' of Miguel de Cervantes," said the barber.

"That Cervantes has been a great friend of mine for many years, and to my knowledge he has had more experience in reverses than in verses. His book has some good invention in it; it raises issues but brings nothing to a conclusion: we'll have to wait for the Second Part it promises — perhaps with revision it may win the full measure of grace now denied it; and in the meantime, señor friend, keep it shut up in your own quarters."

"Very good," said the barber; "and here come three together — the 'Araucana' of Don Alonso de Ercilla, the 'Austriada' of Juan Rufo, Justice of Cordova, and the 'Montserrate' of Christobal de Virués, the Valencian poet."

"These three books," said the curate, "are the best that have been written in Castilian in heroic verse, and they may compare with the most famous of Italy; let them be preserved as the richest treasures of poetry that Spain possesses."

The curate was tired and would not look into any more books, and so decided that, "contents uncertified," all the rest should be burnt; but just then the barber held open one called "The Tears of Angelica."

"I should have shed tears myself," said the curate when he heard the title, "had I ordered that book to be burnt, for its author was one of the famous poets of the world, not just of Spain, and was very happy in his translation of some of Ovid's fables."

title: Part 1, Chapter 7
paragraphs: About the second sally of our worthy knight Don Quixote of La Mancha

At this instant Don Quixote began shouting out, "Here, here, valiant knights! Here is where you need to put forth the might of your strong arms, for those of the Court are gaining the upper hand in the tournament!" Called away by this noise and outcry, they got no further with the inspection of the remaining books, and so it is thought that "The Carolea," "The Lion of Spain," and "The Deeds of the Emperor," written by Don Luis de Ávila, went to the fire unseen and unheard, for they were no doubt among those that remained, and perhaps if the curate had seen them they would not have suffered so severe a sentence.
When they reached Don Quixote he was already out of bed, still shouting and raving, and slashing and cutting all round, as wide awake as if he had never slept.

They closed with him and by force got him back to bed, and once he had calmed down a little, addressing the curate he said, "Truly, Señor Archbishop Turpin, it is a great disgrace for us who call ourselves the Twelve Peers to have so carelessly let the knights of the Court win the victory in this tournament, after we adventurers had carried off the honour on the three previous days."

"Hush, friend," said the curate; "please God, the luck may turn, and what is lost today may be won tomorrow; for now, let your worship take care of your health, since it seems to me you are over-tired, if not badly wounded."

"Wounded, no," said Don Quixote, "but bruised and battered, no doubt, for that bastard Don Roland has cudgelled me with the trunk of an oak tree, and all out of envy, because he sees that I alone rival him in his achievements. But I should not call myself Reinaldos of Montalvan if he does not pay me for it in spite of all his enchantments as soon as I rise from this bed. For now, let them bring me something to eat, for that, I feel, is what would most serve my purpose, and leave the avenging to me."
They did as he wished; they gave him something to eat, and once more he fell asleep, leaving them marvelling at his madness.

That night the housekeeper burnt to ashes all the books that were in the yard and in the whole house, and some must have gone up that deserved preservation in lasting archives; but their fate, and the laziness of the inspector, did not allow it, and so in them was verified the proverb that the innocent suffer for the guilty.

One of the remedies the curate and the barber immediately applied to their friend's disorder was to wall up and plaster over the room where the books had been, so that when he got up he wouldn't find it (the idea being that, the cause removed, the effect might cease), and they would say that some magician had carried it off, room and all. This was done with all dispatch. Two days later Don Quixote got up, and the first thing he did was go and look at his books; and not finding the room where he had left it, he wandered from side to side looking for it. He came to the place where the door had been, and felt at it with his hands, and turned and twisted his eyes in every direction without saying a word; but after a long while he asked his housekeeper whereabouts the room that held his books was.

The housekeeper, who had been well coached in what to answer, said, "What room, or what nothing, is your worship looking for? There is neither room nor books in this house now, for the devil himself has carried it all away."

"It was not the devil," said the niece, "but a magician who came on a cloud one night, the day after your worship left, and dismounting from a serpent he rode he entered the room — what he did in there I don't know — but after a little while he made off, flying through the roof, and left the house full of smoke; and when we went to see what he had done, we found neither book nor room. But the housekeeper and I remember very well that on leaving, the old villain said in a loud voice that, for a private grudge he owed the owner of the books and the room, he had done mischief in that house that would be discovered by and by. He also said his name was the Sage Muñaton."
"He must have said Friston," said Don Quixote.
"I don't know whether he called himself Friston or Friton," said the housekeeper, "only that his name ended in 'ton.'"

"So it does," said Don Quixote, "and he is a sage magician, a great enemy of mine, who has a grudge against me, because he knows by his arts and learning that in the course of time I am to engage in single combat with a knight he befriends, and that I am to defeat him, and he will be unable to prevent it; and for that reason he tries to do me every ill turn he can. But I promise him it will be hard for him to oppose or evade what is decreed by Heaven."

"Who doubts that?" said the niece; "but, uncle, who mixes you up in these quarrels? Wouldn't it be better to stay peacefully at home instead of roaming the world looking for better bread than ever came of wheat, never reflecting that many go for wool and come back shorn?"

"Oh, niece of mine," replied Don Quixote, "how wide of the mark you are in your reckoning: before they shear me I shall have plucked away and stripped off the beards of all who dare to touch so much as the tip of one of my hairs."
The two were unwilling to say anything more, as they could see his anger was kindling.

In short, he stayed quietly at home for fifteen days, showing no signs of wanting to take up his former delusions, and during that time he held lively discussions with his two friends, the curate and the barber, on his contention that what the world most needed was knights-errant, and that in him the revival of knight-errantry was to be accomplished. The curate sometimes contradicted him, sometimes went along with him, for if he had not taken that precaution he would have been unable to bring him to reason at all.

Meanwhile Don Quixote was working on a farm labourer, a neighbour of his, an honest man (if that title can be given to one who is poor), but with very little wit in his pate. In short, he so talked him over, with such persuasions and promises, that the poor clown made up his mind to ride out with him and serve as his squire. Don Quixote, among other things, told him he ought to be willing to go gladly, because any moment an adventure might occur that could win an island in the twinkling of an eye and leave him governor of it. On these and similar promises Sancho Panza (for that was the labourer's name) left wife and children and engaged himself as squire to his neighbour.

Don Quixote next set about raising some money; and by selling one thing, pawning another, and getting a bad bargain in every case, he scraped together a fair sum. He provided himself with a buckler, which he borrowed from a friend, and, patching up his battered helmet as best he could, he warned his squire Sancho of the day and hour he meant to set out, so Sancho could provide himself with what he thought most necessary. Above all, he ordered him to take saddlebags. Sancho said he would, and that he meant to take along a very good ass he had, since he was not much given to going on foot. About the ass, Don Quixote hesitated a little, trying to recall whether any knight-errant had ever taken with him a squire mounted on ass-back; but no example came to mind. Even so, he decided to take him, intending to provide him with a more honourable mount when the chance presented itself, by appropriating the horse of the first discourteous knight he came across. He provided himself with shirts and such other things as he could, following the host's advice; and all this being done, without taking leave — Sancho Panza of his wife and children, or Don Quixote of his housekeeper and niece — they rode out unseen by anyone from the village one night, and made such good progress over the course of it that by daylight they considered themselves safe from discovery even if a search were made.

Sancho rode on his ass like a patriarch, with his saddlebags and wine-flask, longing to see himself soon governor of the island his master had promised him.
