Don Quixote chose to take the same route and road he had taken on his first journey, that over the Campo de Montiel, which he travelled with less discomfort than the previous time; for, as it was early morning and the rays of the sun fell on them at an angle, the heat did not distress them.
And now Sancho Panza said to his master, "Your worship will be careful, Señor Knight-errant, not to forget about the island you've promised me, for be it ever so big I'll be equal to governing it."

To which Don Quixote replied, "You must know, friend Sancho Panza, that it was a very common practice among the knights-errant of old to make their squires governors of the islands or kingdoms they won, and I am determined that on my part there shall be no failure in so liberal a custom; on the contrary, I mean to improve upon it. They sometimes — and perhaps most often — waited until their squires were old, and then, when those squires had had enough of service and hard days and worse nights, they gave them some title or other, count or at most marquis, of some valley or province more or less. But if you live and I live, it may well be that before six days are out I shall have won some kingdom that has others depending on it, which will be just the thing to enable you to be crowned king of one of them. And don't think this remarkable, for things and chances fall to such knights in ways so unexampled and unforeseen that I might easily give you even more than I promise you."
"In that case," said Sancho Panza, "if I became a king by one of those miracles your worship speaks of, even Juana Gutierrez, my old woman, would come to be queen and my children infantes."
"Well, who doubts it?" said Don Quixote.

"I doubt it," replied Sancho Panza, "because for my part I'm convinced that even if God should shower down kingdoms on the earth, not one of them would fit the head of Mari Gutierrez. Let me tell you, señor, she isn't worth two maravedis for a queen; countess will fit her better, and that only with God's help."

"Leave it to God, Sancho," returned Don Quixote, "for he will give her what suits her best; but don't undervalue yourself so far as to be content with anything less than being governor of a province."
"I won't, señor," answered Sancho, "especially as I have a man of your quality for a master in your worship, who will know how to give me everything suitable for me and that I can carry."

title: Part 1, Chapter 8
paragraphs: About the good fortune that the valiant Don Quixote had in the terrible and undreamt-of adventure of the windmills, with other occurrences worthy to be fitly recorded

At this point they came in sight of thirty or forty windmills that stand on that plain, and the moment Don Quixote saw them he said to his squire, "Fortune is arranging matters for us better than we could have wished, for look there, friend Sancho Panza, where thirty or more monstrous giants present themselves, all of whom I mean to engage in battle and slay, and with whose spoils we shall begin to make our fortunes; for this is righteous warfare, and it is God's good service to sweep so evil a breed from the face of the earth."
"What giants?" said Sancho Panza.
"Those you see there," answered his master, "with the long arms — some of them nearly two leagues long."
"Look, your worship," said Sancho; "what we see there aren't giants but windmills, and what look like their arms are the sails — turned by the wind, they make the millstone go."

"It's easy to see," replied Don Quixote, "that you're not used to this business of adventures; those are giants — and if you're afraid, get yourself away from here and take to praying while I engage them in fierce and unequal combat."

So saying, he spurred his steed Rocinante, ignoring the cries his squire Sancho sent after him, warning him that they were most certainly windmills and not giants he was going to attack. He, however, was so sure they were giants that he neither heard Sancho's cries nor perceived what they were, near as he was, but bore down on them shouting, "Don't run, you cowards and vile creatures, for a single knight is attacking you."
A slight breeze sprang up at this moment, and the great sails began to move, seeing which Don Quixote exclaimed, "Though you flourish more arms than the giant Briareus, you have me to reckon with."

So saying, and commending himself with all his heart to his lady Dulcinea, begging her to support him in such peril, with lance in rest and covered by his buckler, he charged at Rocinante's fullest gallop and fell upon the first mill in front of him; but as he drove his lance-point into the sail, the wind whirled it round with such force that it shattered the lance to pieces, sweeping with it horse and rider, who went rolling over on the plain in a sorry condition. Sancho hastened to help him as fast as his ass could go, and when he came up he found him unable to move, with such a shock had Rocinante fallen on top of him.

"God bless me!" said Sancho. "Didn't I tell your worship to mind what you were about, that they were only windmills? No one could have made any mistake about it but someone with the same kind of thing in his head."

"Hush, friend Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "the fortunes of war, more than any other, are subject to frequent fluctuations; and besides, I think — and it is the truth — that that same sage Friston who carried off my study and books has turned these giants into mills in order to rob me of the glory of vanquishing them, such is the enmity he bears me; but in the end his wicked arts will avail little against my good sword."

"God order it as He may," said Sancho Panza, and helping him to rise he got him back up on Rocinante, whose shoulder was half out of joint. Then, discussing the recent adventure, they followed the road to Puerto Lapice, for there, said Don Quixote, they could not fail to find adventures in abundance and variety, as it was a great thoroughfare. For all that, he was much grieved at the loss of his lance, and saying so to his squire, he added, "I remember reading how a Spanish knight, Diego Perez de Vargas by name, having broken his sword in battle, tore from an oak a ponderous bough or branch, and with it did such things that day, and pounded so many Moors, that he earned the surname of Machuca, and he and his descendants from that day forth were called Vargas y Machuca. I mention this because from the first oak I see I mean to rip off such another branch, large and stout like that, with which I am determined and resolved to do such deeds that you may count yourself very fortunate to be found worthy to come and see them, and be eyewitness to things that will scarcely be believed."
"Be that as God will," said Sancho, "I believe it all as your worship says it; but straighten up a little, you seem all on one side, maybe from the shaking of the fall."

"That is the truth," said Don Quixote, "and if I make no complaint of the pain it's because knights-errant are not allowed to complain of any wound, even though their bowels be coming out through it."

"If that's so," said Sancho, "I have nothing to say; but God knows I would rather your worship complained when anything ailed you. For my part, I confess I must complain however small the ache may be — unless this rule about not complaining extends to the squires of knights-errant as well."

Don Quixote could not help laughing at his squire's simplicity, and he assured him he might complain whenever and however he chose, as much as he liked, for so far he had never read of anything to the contrary in the order of knighthood.

Sancho reminded him it was dinner-time, to which his master replied that he wanted nothing himself just then, but that _he_ might eat whenever he had a mind. With this permission Sancho settled himself as comfortably as he could on his beast, and taking out of the saddlebags what he had stowed in them, jogged along behind his master munching deliberately, and from time to time taking a pull at the wine-flask with a relish that the thirstiest tapster in Malaga might have envied; and while he went on this way, gulping down draught after draught, he never gave a thought to any of the promises his master had made him, nor did he reckon it any hardship — rather a recreation — going in quest of adventures, however dangerous they might be. Finally they passed the night among some trees, from one of which Don Quixote plucked a dry branch to serve him, after a fashion, as a lance, and fixed on it the head he had removed from the broken one. All that night Don Quixote lay awake thinking of his lady Dulcinea, in order to conform to what he had read in his books, of how many a night in the forests and deserts knights used to lie sleepless, supported by the memory of their mistresses. Not so did Sancho Panza spend it, for, his stomach being full of something stronger than chicory water, he made one long sleep of it, and if his master had not called him, neither the rays of the sun beating on his face nor all the cheery notes of the birds welcoming the new day would have had power to wake him. On getting up he tried the wine-flask and found it noticeably less full than the night before, which grieved his heart because they did not seem to be on a road that would readily make good the loss. Don Quixote chose not to break his fast, for, as has already been said, he confined himself to savoury memories for nourishment.

They returned to the road they had set out on, the one leading to Puerto Lapice, and at three in the afternoon they came in sight of it. "Here, brother Sancho Panza," said Don Quixote when he saw it, "we may plunge our hands up to the elbows in what they call adventures. But mind — even if you see me in the greatest danger in the world, you must not put a hand to your sword in my defence, unless you can see that those attacking me are common rabble or low folk; in that case you may very properly help me. But if they are knights, it is on no account permitted or allowed to you by the laws of knighthood to help me until you have been dubbed a knight yourself."

"Most certainly, señor," replied Sancho, "your worship shall be obeyed in this to the letter, all the more as I am peaceful by nature and no friend to mixing in strife and quarrels — though it's true that when it comes to defending my own person I won't take much notice of those laws, since laws human and divine allow each one to defend himself against any assailant whatever."
"That I grant," said Don Quixote, "but in the matter of aiding me against knights you must put a restraint on your natural impetuosity."
"I'll do so, I promise," answered Sancho, "and I'll keep this precept as carefully as Sunday."

While they were talking, there appeared on the road two friars of the order of St. Benedict, mounted on two dromedaries — for not less tall were the two mules they rode. They wore travelling spectacles and carried sunshades; and behind them came a coach attended by four or five people on horseback and two muleteers on foot. In the coach was, as later appeared, a Biscay lady on her way to Seville, where her husband was about to take ship for the Indies with an appointment of high honour. The friars, though going the same road, were not in her company; but the moment Don Quixote caught sight of them he said to his squire, "Either I am mistaken, or this is going to be the most famous adventure ever seen, for those black bodies we see over there must be — and doubtless are — magicians who are carrying off some stolen princess in that coach, and with all my might I must right this wrong."

"This will be worse than the windmills," said Sancho. "Look, señor: those are friars of St. Benedict, and the coach plainly belongs to some travellers. I tell you to watch what you're doing and don't let the devil mislead you."
"I have told you already, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "that on the subject of adventures you know little. What I am saying is the truth, as you shall see presently."

So saying, he advanced and posted himself in the middle of the road along which the friars were coming, and as soon as he thought they had come near enough to hear him, he cried aloud, "Devilish and unnatural beings, release at once the highborn princesses you are carrying off by force in this coach, or else prepare to meet a speedy death as the just punishment of your evil deeds."

The friars drew rein and stood wondering at the appearance of Don Quixote as well as at his words, and replied, "Señor Caballero, we are not devilish or unnatural, but two brothers of St. Benedict going about our business, and we do not know whether or not there are any captive princesses coming in this coach."

"No soft words with me, for I know you, lying rabble," said Don Quixote, and without waiting for a reply he spurred Rocinante and with levelled lance charged the first friar with such fury and determination that, if the friar had not flung himself off the mule, he would have brought him to the ground against his will, and sore wounded, if not killed outright. The second brother, seeing how his comrade was being treated, drove his heels into his castle of a mule and made off across the country faster than the wind.

Sancho Panza, when he saw the friar on the ground, dismounted briskly from his ass, rushed at him, and began to strip off his gown. At that instant the friars' muleteers came up and asked what he was stripping him for. Sancho answered that this fell to him lawfully as spoils of the battle his lord Don Quixote had won. The muleteers, who had no sense of humour and did not understand all this about battles and spoils, seeing that Don Quixote was some distance off talking to the travellers in the coach, fell on Sancho, knocked him down, and, leaving hardly a hair in his beard, belaboured him with kicks and left him stretched breathless and senseless on the ground; and without any further delay they helped the friar to mount, who, trembling, terrified, and pale, as soon as he found himself in the saddle, spurred after his companion, who stood at a distance watching the result of the onslaught. Then, not caring to wait for the end of the affair just begun, they pursued their journey, making more crosses than if the devil were after them.

Don Quixote was, as has been said, speaking to the lady in the coach. "Your beauty, lady mine," he said, "may now dispose of your person as may best please you, for the pride of your abductors lies prostrate on the ground through this strong arm of mine; and lest you be pining to know the name of your deliverer, know that I am called Don Quixote of La Mancha, knight-errant and adventurer, and captive to the peerless and beautiful lady Dulcinea del Toboso; and in return for the service you have received from me I ask no more than that you should return to El Toboso, present yourself on my behalf before that lady, and tell her what I have done to set you free."

One of the squires attending the coach, a Biscayan, was listening to everything Don Quixote was saying, and seeing that he would not let the coach go on, but was insisting it must return at once to El Toboso, he charged at him, and seizing his lance addressed him in bad Castilian and worse Biscayan after his fashion, "Begone, caballero, and ill go with thee; by the God that made me, unless thou quittest coach, slayest thee as art here a Biscayan."

Don Quixote understood him perfectly well, and answered very quietly, "If you were a knight, as you are not, I should already have chastised your folly and rashness, you miserable creature." To which the Biscayan returned, "I no gentleman! — I swear to God thou liest as I am Christian: if thou droppest lance and drawest sword, soon shalt thou see thou art carrying water to the cat: Biscayan on land, hidalgo at sea, hidalgo at the devil, and look, if thou sayest otherwise thou liest."

"'"You will see presently," said Agrajes,'" replied Don Quixote; and throwing his lance on the ground he drew his sword, braced his buckler on his arm, and attacked the Biscayan, bent on taking his life.

The Biscayan, seeing him coming on, though he wanted to dismount from his mule — one of those sorry ones let out for hire, in which he had no confidence — had no choice but to draw his sword. Luckily for him, he was near the coach, from which he managed to snatch a cushion that served him as a shield; and they went at each other as though they were two mortal enemies. The others tried to make peace between them, but couldn't, for the Biscayan declared in his garbled speech that if they did not let him finish his battle he would kill his mistress and everyone who tried to stop him. The lady in the coach, amazed and terrified at what she saw, ordered the coachman to draw aside a little, and settled down to watch this fierce struggle, in the course of which the Biscayan dealt Don Quixote a mighty stroke on the shoulder over the top of his buckler, which, given to a man without armour, would have split him to the waist. Don Quixote, feeling the weight of this prodigious blow, cried out, "O lady of my soul, Dulcinea, flower of beauty, come to the aid of this your knight, who, in fulfilling his obligations to your beauty, finds himself in this extreme peril." To say this, to lift his sword, to shelter himself well behind his buckler, and to attack the Biscayan was the work of an instant, determined as he was to venture everything on a single blow. The Biscayan, seeing him come on in this way, was convinced of his courage by his spirited bearing, and resolved to follow his example, so he waited for him keeping well under cover of his cushion, being unable to manoeuvre at all with his mule, which, dead tired and never meant for this kind of game, could not stir a step.

On, then, as I said, came Don Quixote against the wary Biscayan, sword raised and firmly intending to split him in half, while on his side the Biscayan waited for him sword in hand, under the protection of his cushion; and all present stood trembling, waiting in suspense for the result of blows that threatened to fall as they did, and the lady in the coach and the rest of her party were making a thousand vows and offerings to all the images and shrines of Spain, that God might deliver her squire and all of them from this great peril they found themselves in. But it spoils all that at this point and crisis the author of the history leaves the battle hanging, on the excuse that he could find nothing further written about these achievements of Don Quixote than what has already been set out. It is true the second author of this work was unwilling to believe that a history so curious could have been allowed to fall under the sentence of oblivion, or that the wits of La Mancha could have been so undiscerning as not to preserve, in their archives or registries, some documents referring to this famous knight; and this being his conviction, he did not despair of finding the conclusion of this pleasant history — which, heaven favouring him, he did find, in a way to be related in the Second Part.

title: Part 1, Chapter 9
paragraphs: In which the terrific battle between the gallant Biscayan and the valiant Manchegan is brought to an end

In the First Part of this history, we left the valiant Biscayan and the famous Don Quixote with their swords drawn and raised, each ready to deliver a slash so furious that, if the blows had landed squarely, they would at the very least have split both men from head to toe and laid them open like a pomegranate. And at that critical moment, the delightful history simply stopped — cut short, with no hint from the author about where the missing part might be found.

This upset me deeply. The pleasure of having read such a small portion turned to frustration when I considered how slim my chances were of finding the large part of this fascinating tale that seemed to be missing. It struck me as impossible, and contrary to all precedent, that so good a knight should have lacked some sage to take on the job of recording his marvelous achievements. No knight-errant who ever rode out after adventures — so the stories say — was ever without one; every one of them had one or two sages seemingly made for the purpose, who not only recorded their deeds but described their most trivial thoughts and follies, however private they were. Surely a knight this good could not have been so unlucky as to miss out on what Platir and others like him had in abundance. So I could not bring myself to believe that such a gallant tale had been left maimed and mutilated, and I laid the blame on Time, the devourer and destroyer of all things, which had either hidden it or consumed it.

On the other hand, it occurred to me that since his library had contained books as modern as "The Enlightenment of Jealousy" and the "Nymphs and Shepherds of Henares," his story must be modern too, and even if it had never been written down, it might survive in the memories of the people of his village and the surrounding area. This thought kept me restless and longing to know, truly and completely, the whole life and wondrous deeds of our famous Spaniard, Don Quixote of La Mancha — light and mirror of Manchegan chivalry, and the first man in our age, in these wicked days of ours, to devote himself to the work and practice of knight-errantry: righting wrongs, helping widows, and protecting damsels of the kind that used to ride from mountain to mountain and valley to valley on their palfreys, whip in hand, with their virginity entirely intact. In the old days — unless some ruffian, or some peasant with a hood and hatchet, or some monstrous giant forced himself on them — there were damsels who, after eighty years of never once sleeping a night under a roof, went to their graves as untouched as the mothers who bore them. For these reasons and others, I say, our gallant Don Quixote deserves lasting and notable praise — and some should not be withheld even from me, for the labor and trouble I spent searching out the ending of this delightful history. Though I know perfectly well that if Heaven, chance, and good fortune had not helped me, the world would have been deprived of an entertainment and a pleasure that can comfortably fill a couple of hours for anyone who reads it attentively. Here is how the discovery happened.

One day, when I was in the Alcana of Toledo, a boy came up to sell some pamphlets and old papers to a silk merchant. Since I love reading anything — even the scraps of paper lying in the street — that natural inclination of mine led me to pick up one of the pamphlets the boy was selling, and I saw it was written in characters I recognized as Arabic. But although I could recognize them, I couldn't read them, so I looked around for a Spanish-speaking Morisco who could read them to me; and finding such an interpreter was no great difficulty, since I could have found one even for an older and better language. In short, chance supplied me with one, and when I explained what I wanted and put the book in his hands, he opened it in the middle, read for a moment, and began to laugh. I asked him what was so funny, and he answered that it was something written in the margin of the book as a note. I told him to read it to me, and, still laughing, he said, "In the margin, as I said, this is written: 'This Dulcinea del Toboso, so often mentioned in this history, had, they say, the best hand of any woman in all La Mancha for salting pigs.'"

When I heard the name Dulcinea del Toboso, I was stunned and amazed, because it hit me immediately that these pamphlets contained the history of Don Quixote. With that thought, I urged him to read the beginning, and he did, translating the Arabic into Castilian on the spot: "History of Don Quixote of La Mancha, written by Cid Hamete Benengeli, an Arab historian." It took real self-control to hide my joy when the book's title reached my ears. Snatching it away from the silk merchant, I bought all the papers and pamphlets from the boy for half a real — and if the boy had been sharp enough to realize how badly I wanted them, he could easily have counted on making more than six reals from the deal. I immediately withdrew with the Morisco into the cloister of the cathedral and begged him to translate every pamphlet that dealt with Don Quixote into Castilian, leaving nothing out and adding nothing, and offered to pay him whatever he wanted. He settled for two arrobas of raisins and two bushels of wheat, and promised to translate them faithfully and quickly. But to make things easier, and to keep such a precious find from leaving my hands, I brought him to my house, where in little more than a month and a half he translated the whole thing, exactly as it is set down here.

In the first pamphlet, the battle between Don Quixote and the Biscayan was drawn true to life: the two of them posed exactly as the history describes, swords raised, one protected by his buckler and the other by his cushion, and the Biscayan's mule rendered so realistically that you could tell it was a rented one from a bowshot away. Under the Biscayan's feet was an inscription that read, "Don Sancho de Azpeitia," which no doubt must have been his name; and at Rocinante's feet was another that read, "Don Quixote." Rocinante was wonderfully portrayed — so long and thin, so lank and lean, his backbone so prominent and his condition so far gone in consumption that he showed plainly how much judgment and accuracy had gone into giving him the name Rocinante. Near him stood Sancho Panza, holding his donkey's halter, with another label at his feet that read "Sancho Zancas"; judging by the picture, he must have had a big belly, a short body, and long shanks, which is no doubt why he was given the names Panza and Zancas, since the history calls him by both surnames several times. A few other minor details could be mentioned, but they are all of little importance and have nothing to do with the true telling of the history — and no history can be bad as long as it is true.

If any objection is raised against this one on the grounds of its truthfulness, it can only be that its author was an Arab, since lying is a very common habit among people of that nation; though, since they are such enemies of ours, it is more likely that he left things out than that he added things in. That is my own opinion, anyway: wherever he could and should have let his pen run free in praise of so worthy a knight, he seems to me to pass over it in deliberate silence — which is badly done and worse intended, because it is the business and duty of historians to be exact, truthful, and completely free of passion. Neither self-interest nor fear, neither hatred nor love, should make them stray from the path of truth, whose mother is history: the rival of time, the storehouse of deeds, the witness for the past, the example and counsel for the present, and the warning for the future. In this history, I know, the reader will find everything that could be desired in the most agreeable form, and if it falls short in any good quality, I insist the fault lies with its dog of an author and not with the subject. To be brief, its Second Part, according to the translation, began like this:

With their sharp swords raised and poised high in the air, the two valiant and furious combatants seemed to threaten heaven, earth, and hell itself, such was the resolve and determination in their bearing. The fiery Biscayan was the first to strike, and his blow came with such force and fury that, had the sword not turned in mid-stroke, that single blow would have been enough to end this bitter struggle and all the adventures of our knight. But the good fortune that was saving him for greater things turned his adversary's sword aside, so that although it struck him on the left shoulder, it did him no worse harm than to strip that whole side of its armor, carrying away a large piece of his helmet along with half his ear — all of which crashed to the ground in fearful ruin, leaving him in a sorry state.

Good God! Who could properly describe the rage that filled the heart of our Manchegan when he saw himself treated this way? All that can be said is that it was such that he rose up again in his stirrups, gripped his sword more firmly in both hands, and came down on the Biscayan with such fury — striking him full on the cushion and on the head — that even so good a shield proved useless. As if a mountain had fallen on him, the Biscayan began to bleed from his nose, mouth, and ears, reeling as though about to topple backward off his mule, which he certainly would have done if he hadn't thrown his arms around its neck. Even so, his feet slipped out of the stirrups, then his arms lost their hold, and the mule, panicking at the terrible blow, bolted across the plain and with a few bucks threw its master to the ground. Don Quixote stood watching very calmly, and when he saw him fall, he leaped from his horse, ran to him briskly, and, holding the point of his sword to his eyes, ordered him to surrender or he would cut off his head. The Biscayan was so dazed that he couldn't answer a word, and things would have gone badly for him — so blind was Don Quixote's fury — if the ladies in the coach, who until then had been watching the fight in terror, had not hurried over to him and begged him earnestly to grant them the great grace and favor of sparing their squire's life. Don Quixote answered with great gravity and dignity, "In truth, fair ladies, I am quite content to do what you ask of me; but it must be on one condition and understanding: that this knight promise me to go to the village of El Toboso and present himself on my behalf before the peerless lady Dulcinea, so that she may deal with him however pleases her best."
The terrified and distraught ladies, without questioning Don Quixote's demand or asking who Dulcinea might be, promised that their squire would do everything he had been commanded to do.
"Then, on the faith of that promise," said Don Quixote, "I will do him no further harm, though he richly deserves it from me."

title: Part 1, Chapter 10
paragraphs: About the pleasant conversation that passed between Don Quixote and his squire Sancho Panza

By this time Sancho had risen, rather the worse for the handling of the friars' muleteers, and stood watching the battle of his master Don Quixote, praying in his heart that it might be God's will to grant him the victory, and that he might thereby win some island to make him governor of, as he had promised. Seeing, therefore, that the struggle was now over, and that his master was returning to mount Rocinante, he came up to hold the stirrup for him, and before he could mount, he went on his knees before him and, taking his hand, kissed it saying, "May it please your worship, Señor Don Quixote, to give me the government of that island that has been won in this hard fight; for be it ever so big, I feel myself in sufficient force to be able to govern it as much and as well as anyone in the world who has ever governed islands."

To which Don Quixote replied, "You must note, brother Sancho, that this adventure and those like it are not adventures of islands, but of crossroads, in which nothing is won except a broken head or an ear the less: have patience, for adventures will present themselves out of which I may make you not just a governor, but something more."

Sancho gave him many thanks, and again kissing his hand and the skirt of his hauberk, helped him to mount Rocinante, then mounted his ass himself and went on following his master, who at a brisk pace, without taking leave or saying anything further to the ladies in the coach, turned into a wood that was nearby. Sancho followed him at his ass's best trot, but Rocinante stepped out so that, seeing himself left behind, he was forced to call out to his master to wait for him. Don Quixote did so, reining in Rocinante until his weary squire came up, who on reaching him said, "It seems to me, señor, it would be prudent of us to go and take refuge in some church, for, seeing the state you've left the man you fought in, it'll be no wonder if they report it to the Holy Brotherhood and have us arrested, and faith, if they do, before we get out of jail we'll have to sweat for it."
"Peace," said Don Quixote; "where have you ever seen or heard of a knight-errant being arraigned before a court of justice, however many homicides he may have committed?"

"I know nothing about omecils," answered Sancho, "nor in my life have had anything to do with one; I only know that the Holy Brotherhood looks after those who fight in the fields, and in that other matter I don't meddle."

"Then you need have no uneasiness, my friend," said Don Quixote, "for I will deliver you out of the hands of the Chaldeans, much more out of those of the Brotherhood. But tell me, as you live, have you seen a more valiant knight than I in all the known world? Have you read in history of any who has or had higher mettle in attack, more spirit in keeping it up, more dexterity in wounding, or skill in overthrowing?"

"The truth is," answered Sancho, "that I have never read any history, for I can neither read nor write; but what I'll venture to bet is that a more daring master than your worship I have never served in all the days of my life — and God grant that this daring isn't paid for where I have said. What I beg of your worship is to dress your wound, for a great deal of blood is flowing from that ear, and I have here some lint and a little white ointment in the saddlebags."
"All that might be well dispensed with," said Don Quixote, "if I had only remembered to make a vial of the balsam of Fierabras, for one single drop saves time and medicine."
"What vial and what balsam is that?" said Sancho Panza.

"It is a balsam," answered Don Quixote, "the recipe for which I have in my memory, with which you need have no fear of death, nor dread dying of any wound; so when I have made it and given it to you, you have nothing to do, when in some battle you see they have cut me in half through the middle of the body — as is wont to happen frequently — but, neatly and very carefully, before the blood congeals, to place that portion of the body which has fallen to the ground onto the other half which remains in the saddle, taking care to fit it on evenly and exactly. Then you shall give me to drink just two drops of the balsam I have mentioned, and you shall see me become sounder than an apple."

"If that's so," said Panza, "I renounce from this moment the government of the promised island, and want nothing more in payment of my many faithful services than that your worship give me the recipe for this supreme liquor, since I'm convinced it will be worth more than two reals an ounce anywhere, and I want no more to pass the rest of my life in ease and honour. But it remains to be told whether it costs much to make."
"With less than three reals, six quarts of it may be made," said Don Quixote.
"Sinner that I am!" said Sancho, "then why does your worship put off making it and teaching it to me?"

"Peace, friend," answered Don Quixote, "greater secrets I mean to teach you and greater favours to bestow on you; and for the present let's see to the dressing, for my ear pains me more than I would wish."

Sancho took out some lint and ointment from the saddlebags; but when Don Quixote saw his helmet shattered, he was about to lose his senses, and clapping his hand on his sword and raising his eyes to heaven, he said, "I swear by the Creator of all things and the four Gospels in their fullest extent, to do as the great Marquis of Mantua did when he swore to avenge the death of his nephew Baldwin (and that was not to eat bread from a tablecloth, nor embrace his wife, and other points which, though I can't now call them to mind, I here grant as expressed), until I take complete vengeance on whoever has committed such an offence against me."

Hearing this, Sancho said to him, "Your worship should bear in mind, Señor Don Quixote, that if the knight has done what was commanded — to go present himself before my lady Dulcinea del Toboso — he will have done all he was bound to do, and does not deserve further punishment unless he commits some new offence."

"You have said well and hit the point," answered Don Quixote, "and so I recall the oath in so far as it relates to taking fresh vengeance on him; but I make and confirm it anew to lead the life I have described, until such time as I take by force from some knight another helmet such as this, and as good. And do not think, Sancho, that I am raising smoke with straw in doing so, for I have someone to imitate in the matter, since the very same thing happened to a hair in the case of Mambrino's helmet, which cost Sacripante so dear."

"Señor," replied Sancho, "let your worship send all such oaths to the devil, for they are very harmful to salvation and prejudicial to the conscience. Just tell me now: if for several days to come we fall in with no man armed with a helmet, what are we to do? Is the oath to be observed in spite of all the inconvenience and discomfort it will be to sleep in your clothes, and not to sleep in a house, and a thousand other mortifications contained in the oath of that old fool the Marquis of Mantua that your worship is now wanting to revive? Let your worship observe that there are no men in armour travelling on any of these roads — nothing but carriers and carters, who not only do not wear helmets but perhaps never heard tell of them all their lives."
"You're wrong there," said Don Quixote, "for we shan't have been above two hours among these crossroads before we see more men in armour than came to Albraca to win the fair Angelica."
"Enough," said Sancho, "so be it then, and God grant us success, and that the time for winning that island which is costing me so dear may soon come — and then let me die."

"I have told you already, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "not to give yourself any uneasiness on that score; for if an island should fail, there is the kingdom of Denmark, or of Sobradisa, which will fit you as a ring fits the finger — and all the more so because, being on _terra firma_, you'll enjoy yourself there all the better. But let's leave that to its own time; see if you have anything for us to eat in those saddlebags, because we must presently go in quest of some castle where we can lodge tonight and make the balsam I told you of, for I swear to you by God, this ear is giving me great pain."
"I have here an onion and a little cheese and a few scraps of bread," said Sancho, "but they are not fare fit for a valiant knight like your worship."

"How little you know about it," answered Don Quixote. "I would have you know, Sancho, that it is the glory of knights-errant to go without eating for a month, and even when they do eat, that it should be of whatever comes first to hand. This would have been clear to you had you read as many histories as I have, for, though they are very many, in all of them I have found no mention of knights-errant eating, except by accident or at some sumptuous banquets prepared for them, and the rest of the time they passed in dalliance. And though it is plain they could not do without eating, and performing all the other natural functions, because in fact they were men like ourselves, it is plain too that, wandering as they did the most part of their lives through woods and wilds and without a cook, their most usual fare would be rustic food such as you now offer me; so, friend Sancho, do not let what pleases me distress you, and do not try to make a new world or pervert knight-errantry."

"Pardon me, your worship," said Sancho, "for as I cannot read or write, as I said just now, I neither know nor grasp the rules of the profession of chivalry. From now on I will stock the saddlebags with every kind of dried fruit for your worship, since you are a knight; and for myself, as I am not one, I'll furnish them with poultry and other more substantial things."

"I'm not saying, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "that it's mandatory on knights-errant not to eat anything but the fruits you speak of — only that their more usual diet must be those, and certain herbs they found in the fields which they knew, and which I know too."
"A good thing it is," answered Sancho, "to know those herbs, for to my thinking it'll be necessary some day to put that knowledge into practice."

And here, taking out what he said he had brought, the pair made their meal peaceably and sociably. But anxious to find quarters for the night, with all dispatch they finished off their poor dry fare, mounted at once, and made haste to reach some habitation before nightfall; but daylight and the hope of succeeding in their object failed them close by the huts of some goatherds, so they decided to spend the night there. As much as it was a disappointment to Sancho not to have reached a house, it was a satisfaction to his master to sleep under the open sky, for he fancied that each time this happened he performed an act of ownership that helped to prove his chivalry.

title: Part 1, Chapter 11
paragraphs: What happened to Don Quixote with some goatherds

The goatherds welcomed him warmly, and Sancho, after stabling Rocinante and the donkey as best he could, drifted toward the smell rising from some pieces of salted goat simmering in a pot over the fire. He would have liked to test right away whether they were ready to be transferred from the pot to his stomach, but he held back, because the goatherds were already lifting them off the fire. They laid sheepskins on the ground, quickly set out their rough table, and with every sign of genuine goodwill invited the two of them to share what they had. Six of the men who belonged to the fold sat down around the skins, having first, with rustic courtesy, urged Don Quixote to take a seat on a trough they had turned upside down for him. Don Quixote sat, and Sancho stayed on his feet to serve the cup, which was made of horn. Seeing him standing, his master said to him:

"So that you can see, Sancho, the good that knight-errantry carries within itself, and how those who serve in any office of it are on the fast road to being honored and respected by the world, I want you to sit here at my side, in the company of these worthy people, and to be one with me, who am your master and natural lord. Eat from my plate and drink from whatever I drink from, because the same thing can be said of knight-errantry that is said of love: it makes all things level."

"Many thanks," said Sancho, "but I can tell your worship that as long as I have enough to eat, I can eat it just as well, or better, standing up and on my own than seated next to an emperor. And honestly, if the truth has to be told, what I eat in my own corner without ceremony or fuss tastes far better to me, even if it's only bread and onions, than the turkeys at those other tables where I'm forced to chew slowly, drink little, wipe my mouth every minute, and can't sneeze or cough when I want to, or do the other things that come with freedom and privacy. So, señor, as for these honors your worship wants to give me as a servant and follower of knight-errantry, trade them for other things that might be of more use and benefit to me. I acknowledge them as fully received, but I renounce them from this moment until the end of the world."
"Even so," said Don Quixote, "you must sit down, because God exalts the one who humbles himself." And taking him by the arm, he forced him to sit down beside him.

The goatherds understood nothing of this jargon about squires and knights-errant; all they did was eat in silence and stare at their guests, who were packing away fist-sized chunks with great style and appetite. When the meat course was finished, they spread out on the sheepskins a great heap of dried acorns, and beside them they set down half a cheese, harder than if it had been made of mortar. All this time the horn was never idle, for it went around so steadily — now full, now empty, like the bucket of a waterwheel — that it soon drained one of the two wineskins in sight. Once Don Quixote had fully satisfied his appetite, he picked up a handful of the acorns, studied them attentively, and launched into a speech along these lines:

"Happy the age, and happy the time, that the ancients called golden — not because gold, so coveted in this iron age of ours, was gathered without effort in that fortunate era, but because the people who lived then did not know the two words 'mine' and 'thine'! In that blessed age everything was held in common. To win his daily food, no one needed to do any work beyond reaching out a hand and gathering it from the sturdy oaks, which stood there generously inviting him with their sweet, ripe fruit. Clear streams and running brooks offered their delicious, transparent waters in noble abundance. In the clefts of rocks and the hollows of trees, the busy and intelligent bees set up their republics, offering the rich harvest of their fragrant labor to every hand, asking nothing in return. The mighty cork trees, compelled by nothing but their own courtesy, shed the broad, light bark that first served to roof houses propped on rough stakes — a shelter against nothing more than the harshness of the sky. Everything then was peace, everything friendship, everything harmony. The dull blade of the curved plow had not yet dared to tear open and pierce the tender insides of our first mother, who, without being forced, yielded from every part of her broad, fertile bosom everything that could satisfy, sustain, and delight the children who then possessed her. In those days the innocent and beautiful young shepherdess wandered from valley to valley and hill to hill, her hair flowing loose, wearing no more clothing than was needed to modestly cover what modesty requires, and has always required, to be hidden. Their ornaments were not like the ones in use today, heightened by Tyrian purple and silk tortured into endless styles, but woven leaves of green dock and ivy — and in these they went as splendidly and becomingly adorned as our court ladies with all the rare and exotic tricks that idle curiosity has taught them. In those days the heart's thoughts of love dressed themselves simply and naturally, exactly as the heart conceived them, and did not try to recommend themselves with forced, rambling wordiness. Fraud, deceit, and malice had not yet mixed themselves with truth and sincerity. Justice held her ground, untroubled and unassailed by the workings of favor and self-interest, which now damage, twist, and besiege her so badly. Arbitrary rulings had not yet taken root in the judge's mind, because back then there was nothing to judge and no one to be judged. Maidens and modesty, as I have said, wandered wherever they pleased, alone and unescorted, without fear of harm from lawless men or libertine assault; and if they were ruined, it happened by their own will and choice. But now, in this hateful age of ours, not one of them is safe, even if some new labyrinth like the one in Crete were to hide and enclose her — even there the plague of gallantry would find its way to her, seeping through cracks or carried on the air by the zeal of its accursed persistence, and despite all seclusion would lead her to ruin. It was for the defense of these maidens, as time went on and wickedness spread, that the order of knights-errant was founded: to defend young women, to protect widows, and to help orphans and the needy. To this order I belong, brother goatherds, and I thank you for the hospitality and warm welcome you have offered me and my squire. For although by natural law everyone alive is obliged to show favor to knights-errant, still, seeing that you welcomed and feasted me without knowing of this obligation, it is only right that I should thank you for your goodwill with all the goodwill in my power."

Our knight delivered this whole long speech — which could very well have been skipped — because the acorns they gave him reminded him of the golden age, and the impulse seized him to aim all this unnecessary argument at the goatherds, who listened to him open-mouthed in amazement without saying a word in reply. Sancho likewise kept quiet, eating acorns and paying repeated visits to the second wineskin, which they had hung from a cork tree to keep the wine cool.

Don Quixote took longer talking than the supper took to finish. When it was over, one of the goatherds said, "So that your worship, señor knight-errant, can say with even more truth that we show you hospitality willingly and gladly, we'll give you some entertainment and pleasure by having one of our comrades sing. He'll be here soon, and he's a very intelligent young man, deeply in love — and what's more, he can read and write and play the rebec to perfection."

The goatherd had barely finished speaking when the notes of the rebec reached their ears, and shortly afterward the player appeared — a very good-looking young man of about twenty-two. His comrades asked him if he had eaten supper, and when he replied that he had, the one who had already made the offer said to him:

"In that case, Antonio, you might as well do us the favor of singing a little, so that this gentleman, our guest, can see that even in the mountains and woods there are musicians. We've told him about your talents, and we want you to show them and prove we're telling the truth. So, on your life, please sit down and sing that ballad about your love — the one your uncle the prebendary composed for you, the one that was so well liked in town."
"With all my heart," said the young man, and without waiting for any more urging he sat down on the trunk of a felled oak, tuned his rebec, and soon began to sing these words.
ANTONIO'S BALLAD
You love me well, Olalla — I know it for certain, even though your eyes, love's silent tongues, have never told me so with a glance.
Since I know that you know my love, I dare to lay claim to yours: once love stops being a secret, it never needs to feel despair.
It's true, Olalla, that sometimes you have shown all too plainly that your heart is as hard as brass and your snow-white breast is stone.
Yet even so, through your coyness and your fickle moods in between, hope is there — at least the hem of her garment can be seen.
Those glimpses are lures to faith, and to faith in you I hold; kindness cannot make it stronger, and coldness cannot make it cold.
If it's true that love is gentle, then in your gentleness I see something that holds out assurance to my hope of winning you.
If it's true that devotion carries a power to move hearts, then what I show you every single day ought to help my suit along.
Many a time you must have noticed — if you care to notice at all — how I go around on Monday dressed in all my Sunday best.
Love's eyes love to look at brightness; love loves whatever is cheerfully dressed; Sunday or Monday, all I care about is that you see me at my best.
I make no mention of the dances, or of the tunes that pleased you so, keeping you awake from midnight until the roosters began to crow;
Or of how I swore outright that no one is as fair as you; it's true, but for saying it the girls all hate me now.
For Teresa of the hillside was stung by my praise of you; she said, "You think you love an angel; it's a monkey you adore;
"Caught by all her glittering trinkets and her borrowed braids of hair, and a whole array of made-up beauties that would snare Love himself."
It was a lie, and I told her so; at that, her cousin threw down a challenge over it — and what followed, you have heard.
Mine is no high-flown affection, mine no passion _par amours_ — as they call it — what I offer is an honest love, and a pure one.
The holy Church has cunning cords, cords made of the softest silk; put your neck beneath the yoke, my dear, and mine will follow — you will see.
Otherwise — and once and for all I swear it by the most renowned of saints — if I ever leave these mountains, it will be in a friar's gown.

Here the goatherd brought his song to a close, and although Don Quixote begged him to sing more, Sancho had no mind for it, being more inclined toward sleep than toward listening to songs. So he said to his master, "Your worship would do well to settle right now where you mean to spend the night, because the work these good men do all day long doesn't allow them to spend the night singing."
"I take your meaning, Sancho," replied Don Quixote. "I can see clearly that those visits to the wineskin demand payment in sleep rather than in music."
"It tastes sweet to all of us, God be blessed," said Sancho.

"I don't deny it," replied Don Quixote, "but settle yourself wherever you like. Those of my calling are more fittingly occupied keeping watch than sleeping. Still, it would be a good idea if you dressed this ear of mine again, because it's giving me more pain than it should."

Sancho did as he was told, but one of the goatherds, seeing the wound, told him not to worry, since he would apply a remedy that would heal it quickly. Gathering some rosemary leaves, which grew there in great quantity, he chewed them, mixed them with a little salt, applied them to the ear, and bound them firmly in place with a bandage, assuring him that no other treatment would be needed — and so it proved.
